    Glossary · Years 1 and 2

    The language of A-level pure maths

    303 terms in plain English, for Year 1 and Year 2 together. Each has an example, a warning about common slips where there is one, the reverse side of the idea, and where it is taught in this book.

    A-level Maths Book / Glossary

    How to use it: terms are in alphabetical order. Each entry shows Year 1 or Year 2. Choose an area of maths (such as Algebra and functions) to see one area, search for a word, or jump to a letter.

    Jump to: A B C D E F G H I L M N O P Q R S T U V W X Y Z

    A

    Addition formulae (compound angle formulae) Trigonometry Year 2

    Formulae for the sine, cosine or tangent of two angles added together or subtracted. They use the sine, cosine or tangent of each angle on its own.

    Examples:sin(A+B)=sinAcosB+cosAsinBsin(A−B)=sinAcosB−cosAsinBcos(A+B)=cosAcosB−sinAsinBcos(A−B)=cosAcosB+sinAsinBtan(A+B)=tanA+tanB1−tanAtanBtan(A−B)=tanA−tanB1+tanAtanBExact value: sin(75°)=sin(45°+30°)=22×32+22×12=6+24.

    Watch out: sin(A+B) is not sinA+sinB. You cannot find the sine of a sum by adding two sines. In the cosine formulae, the sign on the right-hand side is the opposite of the sign inside the bracket.

    Flip it: Putting B=A in the formulae for sin(A+B), cos(A+B) and tan(A+B) gives the Double-angle formulae.

    See also: Double-angle formulae, R-form (harmonic form)

    algebraic fraction Algebra and functions Year 2

    A fraction with algebraic expressions on the top, the bottom or both.

    Examples:x2−1x2+x=(x−1)(x+1)x(x+1)=x−1x, for x≠−1 and x≠0.

    Watch out: Cancel only factors that multiply the whole top and the whole bottom. x+2x does not simplify to 3. State any value that makes the bottom 0.

    Flip it: To add fractions, use a common denominator. To split one fraction back into simple ones, use partial fractions.

    See also: partial fractions, improper algebraic fraction, polynomial

    Ambiguous case Trigonometry Year 1

    Two sides and an angle that is not between them can fit two different triangles. Then the sine rule gives two possible angles.

    Examples:Triangle ABC has A = 30°, a = 7 and b = 10. The sine rule gives sinB=10sin(30°)7=57.So B = 45.6° or B = 180° − 45.6° = 134.4°. Both work, because 30° + 134.4° is less than 180°. There are two triangles.

    Watch out: Two angles have the same sine: sinθ=sin(180°−θ). Always check whether the second angle fits in the triangle (the three angles must add to 180°). If it does not fit, there is only one triangle.

    See also: Sine rule

    Amplitude Trigonometry Year 1

    For a sine or cosine graph, the distance from the middle line of the graph to its highest (or lowest) point.

    Examples:y=3sinx has amplitude 3: it goes between −3 and 3.y=3sinx+1 also has amplitude 3. The graph goes between −2 and 4, and its middle line is y=1.

    Watch out: Amplitude is half the full height, not the full height. A negative number in front, as in y=−3sinx, still gives amplitude 3 (the graph is turned upside down). The tan graph has no amplitude, because it has no highest point.

    See also: Period, R-form (harmonic form)

    Angle in a semicircle Coordinate geometry Year 1

    The angle at a point on a circle, between lines drawn to the two ends of a diameter, is always 90 degrees.

    Examples:On x2+y2=25, take A (-5, 0), B (5, 0) and P (3, 4).Gradient of AP: 48=12. Gradient of PB: −42=−2.The product is −1, so AP and PB are perpendicular.

    Watch out: AB must be a diameter, so it must pass through the centre.

    Flip it: If a triangle has a right angle, the side opposite it is a diameter of the circle through all three corners. The centre of that circle is the midpoint of that side.

    See also: Diameter, Perpendicular, Midpoint

    Angle of inclination Coordinate geometry Year 1

    The angle a line makes with the positive x-axis, measured anticlockwise.

    Example: A line with gradient 0.75 has tanθ=0.75, so θ=tan−10.75=36.9° to 1 decimal place.

    Watch out: A line that goes down to the right has a negative gradient, and your calculator gives a negative angle. Add 180 degrees to get the angle of inclination. Gradient −1: the calculator gives −45°, so the angle of inclination is −45°+180°=135°.

    Flip it: The gradient is the tangent of the angle: m=tanθ. The angle is the inverse tangent of the gradient.

    See also: Gradient

    antiderivative Integration Year 1

    A function whose derivative is a given function.

    Example: x3 is an antiderivative of 3x2. So are x3+5 and x3−2, because they all differentiate to 3x2.

    Watch out: A function has many antiderivatives. They differ only by a constant. The indefinite integral includes all of them by writing +c.

    Flip it: The derivative of an antiderivative is the original function.

    See also: integrate, constant of integration, fundamental theorem of calculus

    Taught in: Integration as reverse differentiation

    Arc Trigonometry Year 2

    A part of the circumference of a circle: the curved line between two points on the circle.

    Example: Two points on a circle split it into a short arc (the minor arc) and a long arc (the major arc). An angle θ at the centre cuts off an arc.

    Watch out: The arc is a curve, so its length is measured along the curve. The straight line joining its ends is the chord, and it is shorter.

    See also: Arc length, Sector, Radian, Segment of a circle

    Arc length Trigonometry Year 2

    The distance along a curved part of a circle's edge. It equals the radius multiplied by the angle at the centre, in radians.

    Examples:s=rθHere s is the arc length, r is the radius and θ is the angle at the centre, in radians.A circle has radius 6 cm. An arc has angle π3 at the centre. s=6×π3=2×π cm, which is 6.28 cm to 3 significant figures.

    Watch out: The angle θ must be in radians. With degrees the formula is s=θ360×2×π×r.

    Flip it: If you know the arc length and the radius, then θ=sr. That is the meaning of a radian: an arc as long as the radius.

    See also: Radian, Arc, Area of a sector

    area below the axis Integration Year 1

    Where a curve is below the x-axis, its definite integral is negative. The area is the same number without the minus sign.

    Examples:For y=x2−4: ∫02(x2−4)dx=233−4×2=−163. The area is 163.From 0 to 3 the curve is below the axis from 0 to 2 and above from 2 to 3. The integral from 2 to 3 is 73. The total area is 163+73=233. The integral from 0 to 3 is −3, which is not the area, because the part below the axis and the part above it partly cancel.

    Watch out: Do not integrate across a point where the curve crosses the x-axis and call the answer an area. Find where the curve crosses the x-axis, integrate each part, and add the areas as positive numbers.

    See also: area under a curve, definite integral, area between two curves

    area between two curves Integration Year 1

    The area enclosed by two curves. It equals the integral of the upper curve minus the lower curve, between the x-values where the curves meet.

    Example: The line y=x+2 and the curve y=x2 meet at x=−1 and x=2. The line is above the curve between them. Area: ∫−12(x+2−x2)dx=92.

    Watch out: Solve the two equations together to find the limits. Subtract the lower curve from the upper curve. If the curves cross between the limits, split the integral there. This method also works when both curves are below the axis.

    See also: area under a curve, definite integral, limits of integration

    Area of a sector Trigonometry Year 2

    The area of the slice of a circle between two radii. It equals half the radius squared multiplied by the angle at the centre, in radians.

    Examples:A=12r2θHere A is the area, r is the radius and θ is the angle at the centre, in radians.Radius 6 cm and angle π3: A=12×36×π3=6×π cm², which is 18.8 cm² to 3 significant figures.

    Watch out: The angle θ must be in radians. Do not forget the half.

    Flip it: When θ=2×π, the sector is the whole circle, and the formula gives πr2.

    See also: Sector, Arc length, Radian, Segment of a circle

    Area of a triangle, ½ab sin C Trigonometry Year 1

    The area of any triangle is half the product of two sides and the sine of the angle between them.

    Example: Two sides are 8 cm and 5 cm and the angle between them is 30°. Area=12×8×5×sin(30°)=10 cm².

    Watch out: The angle must lie between the two sides you use. With the wrong angle the answer is wrong.

    Flip it: If you know the area, one side and the angle between the two sides, rearrange the formula to find the other side.

    See also: Sine rule, Cosine rule

    area under a curve Integration Year 1

    The area between a curve and the x-axis, from one x-value to another. When the curve is above the x-axis, this area equals the definite integral.

    Example: The area under y=x2 from x=0 to x=3 is ∫03x2dx=9 square units.

    Watch out: Where the curve is below the axis, the integral is negative but the area is positive. Split at the points where the curve crosses the axis. See area below the axis.

    Flip it: Differentiating the area function gives the height of the curve.

    See also: definite integral, area below the axis, area between two curves, integration as the limit of a sum

    Arithmetic sequence Sequences and series Year 2

    A sequence in which you add the same number each time to get the next term.

    Examples:3, 7, 11, 15 … adds 4 each time.The nth term is un=a+(n−1)d, where a is the first term and d is the common difference. Here un=3+4(n−1)=4n−1.

    Watch out: It is (n−1)d, not nd. There is one fewer step than the position number. Check with n = 1: you must get a.

    Flip it: A sequence is arithmetic if the difference between each term and the one before is the same number.

    See also: Common difference, Arithmetic series

    Arithmetic series Sequences and series Year 2

    The sum of the terms of an arithmetic sequence.

    Examples:The sum of the first n terms is Sn=n2(2a+(n−1)d), or Sn=n2(a+l), where l is the last term.3+7+11+15+19: n = 5, so S5=52(3+19)=55.The sum 1 + 2 + … + 100 is 1002(1+100)=5050.

    Watch out: Use the right n. If a question gives the last term, work out how many terms there are first: n=l−ad+1.

    Flip it: Why it works: write the sum forwards and backwards and add. Every pair totals a+l, and there are n pairs, so 2Sn=n(a+l).

    See also: Arithmetic sequence, Sum of the first n terms, S_n, Sigma notation

    Ascending powers Sequences and series Year 1

    Written with the lowest power of x first: the constant term, then x, then x squared, and so on.

    Example: 1+6x+12x2+8x3 is in ascending powers of x.

    Watch out: "The first three terms in ascending powers of x" means the three terms with the lowest powers. For (2+x)5, the first term is 25=32, then comes the term in x.

    See also: Binomial expansion

    asymptote Algebra and functions Year 1

    A line that a curve gets closer and closer to as the curve goes off towards very large positive or very large negative values of x or y.

    Examples:y=1x has two asymptotes: the y-axis, x=0, and the x-axis, y=0.y=1x−2+3 has asymptotes x=2 and y=3.

    Watch out: Draw an asymptote as a dashed line and write its equation. It is not part of the curve. Some curves can cross a horizontal asymptote, though y=1x never does.

    See also: reciprocal graph, translation (of a graph)

    axis of symmetry Algebra and functions Year 1

    The vertical line through the vertex of a parabola. It splits the curve into two halves that are mirror images.

    Examples:For y=x2−4x+3, the roots are 1 and 3. The axis of symmetry is halfway between them: x=2.For y=ax2+bx+c the axis is x=−b2a.

    Watch out: It is a line, so write its equation, x=2, and not only the number 2.

    See also: vertex (of a parabola), parabola, root (of an equation or function)

    B

    Base Exponentials and logs Year 1

    The number that is raised to a power. It is also the small number written below log in a logarithm.

    Examples:In 25=32 the base is 2 and the power is 5.In log232=5 the base of the logarithm is 2. It is the same 2.

    Watch out: The base of a logarithm is written small and lower, as in log2x. If no base is written, logx usually means base 10. Check what the question says.

    See also: Exponential function, Logarithm (log), Common logarithm (log base 10), Natural logarithm (ln)

    Binomial expansion Sequences and series Year 1

    Writing (a + b) to a whole-number power n as a sum of n + 1 terms, using the binomial coefficients nCr.

    Examples:(1+2x)3=1+3(2x)+3(2x)2+(2x)3=1+6x+12x2+8x3.The term in an−rbr is Crn an−rbr.

    Watch out: Write brackets round the whole second term: (2x)2=4x2, not 2x2. In (a−b)n the signs alternate. There are always n + 1 terms.

    Flip it: The coefficients in a binomial expansion are the numbers in Pascal’s triangle.

    See also: nCr (binomial coefficient), Pascal’s triangle, Ascending powers, Binomial expansion for any rational power

    Binomial expansion for any rational power Sequences and series Year 2

    The expansion of (1 + x) to a power n that is negative or a fraction. It goes on for ever and is only valid for some values of x.

    Examples:(1+x)n=1+nx+n(n−1)2!x2+n(n−1)(n−2)3!x3 …(1+x)−1=1−x+x2−x3 … for |x|<1.(1+x)1/2=1+12x−18x2 … for |x|<1.For (a+bx)n, factor out an first: an(1+bax)n.

    Watch out: The expansion does not stop, so it is only an approximation if you keep a few terms. For a whole-number power n it stops at the term in xn and is true for every x. If the bracket is (a+bx)n with a not 1, you must factor out an before using the formula.

    See also: Binomial expansion, Range of validity

    Bounds for a root (accuracy) Numerical methods Year 2

    The two values, one below and one above a root, that prove the root is correct to a stated number of decimal places.

    Examples:Show that the root of x3−x−1=0 is 1.32 to 2 decimal places. Numbers that round to 1.32 lie between 1.315 and 1.325.f(1.315)=−0.041 and f(1.325)=0.001. There is a change of sign, so the root is between 1.315 and 1.325. So it is 1.32 to 2 decimal places.

    Watch out: Use the values halfway between the answer and the numbers either side of it (here 1.315 and 1.325), not 1.31 and 1.33. Work out f at these bounds, not at the answer itself.

    See also: Change of sign, Numerical method

    C

    Cartesian equation Coordinate geometry Year 2

    An equation connecting x and y directly, with no parameter.

    Example: From x=2t and y=t2: t=x2, so y=x24.

    Watch out: The Cartesian equation can describe more than the parametric equations do. x=cost,y=cost gives y=x, but the curve is only the part with −1≤x≤1. State any restriction on x or y.

    See also: Parametric equations, Eliminate the parameter

    CAST diagram Trigonometry Year 1

    A diagram of the four quadrants that shows which of sine, cosine and tangent are positive in each one.

    Examples:In the 1st quadrant (0° to 90°) all three are positive. In the 2nd (90° to 180°) only sine is positive. In the 3rd (180° to 270°) only tangent is positive. In the 4th (270° to 360°) only cosine is positive.Solve sinx=0.5 for 0°≤x≤360°. Sine is positive in the 1st and 2nd quadrants. So x = 30° or x = 180° − 30° = 150°.

    Watch out: Start from the acute angle (the angle between the radius and the x-axis), then use the diagram to decide the sign and which quadrants to use.

    See also: Trigonometric equation, Unit circle, Principal value

    Centre of a circle Coordinate geometry Year 1

    The fixed point that is the same distance from every point on the circle.

    Example: The circle (x−2)2+(y−1)2=4 has centre (2, 1). The circle (x+3)2+(y−5)2=9 has centre (-3, 5).

    Watch out: The signs in the equation are the opposite of the coordinates. (x+3) means x−(−3), so the x-coordinate of the centre is −3.

    Flip it: The centre of a circle is the midpoint of any diameter.

    See also: Circle, Equation of a circle, Diameter

    chain rule Differentiation Year 2

    The rule for differentiating a function of a function: differentiate the outer function, then multiply by the derivative of the inner function.

    Examples:dydx=dydu×dudxFor y=(3x+1)5, let u=3x+1. Then y=u5, so dydu=5u4 and dudx=3.So dydx=15(3x+1)4.

    Watch out: The usual slip is to forget to multiply by the derivative of the inner function. Differentiating sin(2x) gives 2cos(2x), not cos(2x).

    Flip it: Integration by substitution and the reverse chain rule undo the chain rule.

    See also: product rule, quotient rule, connected rates of change, implicit differentiation

    Change of base Exponentials and logs Year 1

    A formula that writes a logarithm in one base as one logarithm divided by another, both in a new base.

    Examples:logax=logbxlogbalog220=log1020log102=4.32 to 3 significant figures. Use it to find a logarithm to a base your calculator has no key for.

    Watch out: Not every exam board asks for this formula by name. Check your specification. If the formula is not required, you can still get the same result by taking logarithms of both sides.

    See also: Logarithm (log), Common logarithm (log base 10), Natural logarithm (ln), Exponential equation

    Change of sign Numerical methods Year 2

    Suppose a continuous function is positive at one end of an interval and negative at the other. Then it equals zero somewhere in between, so there is a root there.

    Examples:f(x)=x3−x−1. f(1)=−1 and f(2)=5. The signs are different, so there is a root between 1 and 2.f(1.3)=−0.103 and f(1.4)=0.344. So there is a root between 1.3 and 1.4. Keep narrowing the interval to get more decimal places.

    Watch out: To use it, say: f is continuous, f(a) is negative, f(b) is positive, so there is a root between a and b. The method can fail in two ways. First, f has a Discontinuity in the interval. Second, the interval holds two roots, so the signs at the ends are the same. A root where the graph only touches the x-axis shows no sign change.

    Flip it: To prove a root is correct to a given number of decimal places, find a change of sign between the two bounds: see Bounds for a root (accuracy).

    See also: Continuous function, Discontinuity, Bounds for a root (accuracy), Numerical method

    changing the limits Integration Year 2

    In a definite integral with a substitution, replacing the x-limits with the matching u-limits, found by putting each x-limit into the substitution.

    Example: For ∫012x(x2+1)3dx with u=x2+1: when x=0, u=1. When x=1, u=2. So the integral is ∫12u3du=244−14=154.

    Watch out: Do not mix the two: u-limits go with u, and x-limits go with x. If you change the limits, do not change back to x afterwards.

    See also: integration by substitution, limits of integration, definite integral

    Chord Coordinate geometry Year 1

    A straight line segment joining two points on a circle.

    Example: The points (-4, 3) and (4, 3) are on x2+y2=25. The chord between them has length 8.

    Watch out: A diameter is a chord, and it is the longest chord. Most chords do not go through the centre.

    Flip it: A line that meets a circle at two points cuts the circle in a chord.

    See also: Diameter, Perpendicular from the centre to a chord, Line meeting a circle

    chord of a curve Differentiation Year 1

    A straight line segment that joins two points on a curve.

    Example: On y=x2, the chord from (1, 1) to (3, 9) has gradient 9−13−1=4. The gradient of the curve at x=1 is 2, so the chord is steeper than the curve there.

    Watch out: The gradient of a chord is an average gradient between two points. It is not the gradient of the curve at either point.

    Flip it: Move the second point towards the first and the chord becomes the tangent. See differentiation from first principles.

    See also: differentiation from first principles, gradient of a curve, limit

    Circle Coordinate geometry Year 1

    The set of all points in a plane that are the same distance from one fixed point, called the centre.

    Example: The points (3, 4), (-5, 0) and (0, -5) are all 5 away from the origin, so they lie on the circle x2+y2=25.

    Watch out: A circle is the curve only, not the space inside it. The inside is where x2+y2<25.

    See also: Centre of a circle, Radius, Equation of a circle

    Cobweb diagram Numerical methods Year 2

    A graph of y = g(x) and y = x that shows an iteration spiralling in towards (or out from) a fixed point, with the values alternating either side of the fixed point.

    Examples:It is drawn in the same way as a Staircase diagram: up or down to the curve, across to the line y=x, and repeat.For g(x)=cosx, the lines spiral inwards to the fixed point x=0.739. The values are 0.98, 0.56, 0.85, 0.66, 0.79 … (above, below, above, below).

    Watch out: A cobweb appears when the curve slopes downwards at the fixed point (negative gradient). A spiral that closes in means convergence; a spiral that opens out means divergence.

    See also: Staircase diagram, Convergence, Divergence, Fixed point

    coefficient Algebra and functions Year 1

    The number that multiplies a letter, or a power of a letter, in a term.

    Examples:In 5x3, the coefficient of x3 is 5.In 2x2−7x+4, the coefficient of x is −7, with its sign.

    Watch out: Include the sign. In x2−x the coefficient of x is −1. When no number is written, the coefficient is 1.

    See also: polynomial, constant term, degree (of a polynomial)

    Collinear Vectors Year 1

    Points that all lie on one straight line.

    Examples:Show that A (1, 1), B (3, 2) and C (7, 4) are collinear.AB→ = (21) and BC→ = (42) = 2AB→.The vectors are parallel and share the point B, so A, B and C are collinear.

    Watch out: Parallel is not enough. Two parallel vectors on different lines would not make the points collinear. Say that the vectors share a point.

    See also: Parallel vectors, Vector proof

    Column vector Vectors Year 1

    A vector written as numbers in a column inside brackets. The top number is the move across (in the x direction) and the bottom number is the move up (in the y direction).

    Examples:(32) means 3 across and 2 up.(−14) means 1 to the left and 4 up.

    Watch out: A column vector is a move, not a place. It is not a fraction and it is not the point (3, 2). The point (3, 2) is where you end up if you start at the origin.

    See also: Component, i and j notation, Position vector

    Common difference Sequences and series Year 2

    The fixed number added each time in an arithmetic sequence, written d. It can be negative.

    Example: 20, 17, 14, 11 … has d=17−20=−3.

    Watch out: Take a term minus the one before it: u2−u1. The other way round gives the wrong sign.

    See also: Arithmetic sequence, Common ratio

    Common logarithm (log base 10) Exponentials and logs Year 1

    The logarithm to base 10, which is what the log key on a calculator gives.

    Examples:log101000=3, log100.01=−2, log105=0.699 to 3 decimal places.Solve 10x=500: x=log10500=2.70 to 3 significant figures.

    Watch out: It is often written lg or log with no base. It is not the natural logarithm ln, which is base e.

    See also: Logarithm (log), Natural logarithm (ln)

    Common ratio Sequences and series Year 2

    The fixed number you multiply by each time in a geometric sequence, written r. It can be a fraction or negative.

    Example: 81, 27, 9, 3 … has r=2781=13. 5, −10, 20 … has r=−2.

    Watch out: Divide a term by the one before it. Subtracting finds the common difference instead.

    See also: Geometric sequence, Common difference, Sum to infinity

    completing the square Algebra and functions Year 1

    Rewriting a quadratic in the form a(x minus p) squared plus q. The turning point is then (p, q).

    Examples:x2+6x+5=(x+3)2−4. The vertex is at (−3,−4).2x2+8x+3=2(x+2)2−5. Factor out the 2 from the first two terms.

    Watch out: Halve the coefficient of x, then subtract the square of that half to balance. Also (x+3)2 has its vertex at x=−3, not 3.

    Flip it: Expanding a(x−p)2+q takes you back to ax2+bx+c.

    See also: vertex (of a parabola), quadratic formula, quadratic

    Component Vectors Year 1

    One of the numbers that make up a vector: how far it goes along each axis.

    Examples:The vector (3−2) has x-component 3 and y-component −2.A vector of magnitude 10 at 30° above the x-axis has components 10cos30°=8.66 across and 10sin30°=5 up.

    Watch out: Components can be negative. A negative x-component means the vector points to the left.

    Flip it: Use Pythagoras on the components to find the Magnitude.

    See also: Column vector, Magnitude, Direction of a vector

    composite function Algebra and functions Year 2

    A function made by applying one function and then another. The notation gf(x) means: apply f first, then g.

    Examples:f(x)=2x+1 and g(x)=x2.gf(x)=g(2x+1)=(2x+1)2.fg(x)=f(x2)=2x2+1. This is different.

    Watch out: Read gf(x) from the right. The function nearest to x acts first. Also gf and fg are usually different.

    Flip it: A function followed by its inverse changes nothing: f−1f(x)=x.

    See also: function, inverse function, domain, range (of a function)

    concave Differentiation Year 2

    A curve that bends downwards on an interval, like the top of a hill. A negative second derivative on an interval shows that the curve is concave there.

    Example: For y=−x2, d2ydx2=−2, which is negative. The curve is concave everywhere. Any chord lies below the curve.

    Watch out: Some books say "concave down" for concave and "concave up" for convex. Check the meaning when you read another book. In this book, concave means the curve bends downwards.

    Flip it: Convex is the opposite: it bends upwards.

    See also: convex, second derivative, point of inflection

    conjecture Proof Year 1

    A statement that looks true from examples but has not yet been proved.

    Examples:Goldbach’s conjecture: every even number greater than 2 is the sum of two primes.It works for every number ever checked. No one has proved it.

    Watch out: A conjecture is not a fact. It becomes a fact when someone proves it, and it is rejected when someone finds a counterexample.

    See also: proof, counterexample, statement

    conjugate (of a surd expression) Algebra and functions Year 1

    The partner of an expression such as a plus root b: the same terms with the sign between them changed, so a minus root b.

    Examples:The conjugate of 3+5 is 3−5.(3+5)(3−5)=9−5=4. The product has no surd.

    Watch out: Change only the sign between the two terms. The conjugate of 3+25 is 3−25.

    Flip it: Multiplying an expression by its conjugate always gives a difference of two squares: (a+b)(a−b)=a2−b2.

    See also: rationalise the denominator, surd

    connected rates of change Differentiation Year 2

    Rates of change of two or more quantities that are linked by a formula, so you can use the chain rule to find one rate from another.

    Examples:A circular ripple has radius r cm and area A=π×r2. The radius grows at drdt=2 cm per second.dAdt=dAdr×drdt=2×π×r×2=4×π×r.When r=5, the area grows at 20×π cm² per second.

    Watch out: Write the chain rule first. Put numbers in only after differentiating. A quantity that is shrinking has a negative rate. Check the units.

    See also: chain rule, rate of change

    consecutive integers Proof Year 1

    Integers that follow each other, with each one 1 more than the one before.

    Examples:Three consecutive integers: n, n+1, n+2.Two consecutive even numbers: 2n and 2n+2.

    Watch out: Consecutive integers go up in ones. The integers n and n + 2 are not consecutive. The numbers 2n and 2n+2 are consecutive even numbers, not consecutive integers.

    See also: even number, odd number, integer, proof by deduction

    constant of integration Integration Year 1

    The unknown number c that you add when you integrate without limits. It is there because every constant differentiates to zero.

    Examples:∫2xdx=x2+c.A curve has dydx=2x and passes through (1, 5). So y=x2+c. Put in the point: 5=1+c, so c=4. The curve is y=x2+4.

    Watch out: Forgetting +c is a common way to lose marks. In a definite integral the constant cancels, so you do not write it.

    See also: indefinite integral, antiderivative, general solution

    Taught in: Integration as reverse differentiation

    constant term Algebra and functions Year 1

    The term with no letter in it. It is the value of the polynomial when x is 0.

    Examples:In x3−2x+5, the constant term is 5.The curve y=x3−2x+5 crosses the y-axis at (0,5).

    Watch out: The constant term includes its sign. In x2+3x−4 it is −4.

    See also: polynomial, coefficient

    Continuous function Numerical methods Year 2

    A function whose graph on an interval has no gaps or jumps, so you can draw it without lifting your pen.

    Examples:f(x)=x2−3 is continuous for every x. f(x)=sinx and f(x)=ex are continuous too.f(x)=1x is not continuous on an interval that includes x=0. It has a break there.

    Watch out: A function can be continuous on one interval and not on another. For example 1x is continuous on 1≤x≤2. Always say on which interval.

    Flip it: A break in the graph is called a Discontinuity.

    See also: Discontinuity, Change of sign

    Continuous growth model (rate proportional to size) Exponentials and logs Year 2

    A model in which the rate of change of a quantity is proportional to the quantity itself. It gives exponential growth or decay with base e.

    Examples:dPdt=kP says that the rate of growth of P is k times P. Its solution is P=P0ekt, where P0 is the starting value.If k>0, the quantity grows. If k<0, it decays. For k=−0.2, the half-life is ln20.2=3.47 time units (the same units as t).

    Watch out: Here k is a rate, not a factor. A fixed percentage per step is multiplied (factor b), while k is a continuous rate (a factor of ek each step).

    Flip it: The same idea in reverse: if P=P0ekt, then dPdt=kP, because the derivative of ekt is kekt.

    See also: Exponential growth, Exponential decay, Natural exponential function (e^x), The number e

    Convergence Numerical methods Year 2

    When the values given by an iteration get closer and closer to one number, called the limit.

    Examples:xn+1=cosxn from x0=0.2: the values go 0.98, 0.56, 0.85, 0.66, 0.79 … and settle on 0.739. This is convergence.The limit L satisfies L=g(L). That is how you can find the exact limit or check it.

    Watch out: Convergence is a property of the iteration and the starting value. Start close enough to the limit. Then the iteration is sure to converge when the gradient of g at the limit is between −1 and 1. If that gradient is exactly 1 or −1, this test cannot tell you. If the gradient is positive, the values approach from one side, as in a Staircase diagram. If it is negative, the values go either side of the limit, as in a Cobweb diagram.

    Flip it: The opposite is Divergence.

    See also: Divergence, Fixed point, Staircase diagram, Cobweb diagram

    Convergent Sequences and series Year 2

    A sequence or series that settles on one fixed value. The terms of a sequence get closer to a limit, or the sums of a series get closer to one number.

    Examples:The sequence 1, 12, 14, 18 … converges to 0.The series 1+12+14+18 … converges to 2.

    Watch out: For a series it is not enough that the terms get smaller. The series 1+12+13+14 … has terms that shrink towards 0, but its sum grows without limit.

    Flip it: A sequence or series that does not settle is Divergent.

    See also: Divergent, Limit of a sequence, Sum to infinity

    converse Proof Year 1

    The statement you get by swapping the "if" part and the "then" part of a statement.

    Examples:Statement: if x is 3, then x2=9. Its converse: if x2=9, then x is 3.The statement is true. The converse is false, because x could be −3.

    Watch out: A true statement can have a false converse. Never assume the converse is true.

    See also: implies (⇒), if and only if (⇔), counterexample

    convex Differentiation Year 2

    A curve that bends upwards on an interval, like a bowl. A positive second derivative on an interval shows that the curve is convex there.

    Example: For y=x2, d2ydx2=2, which is positive. The curve is convex everywhere. Any chord lies above the curve.

    Watch out: Some books say "concave up" for convex. Convex is about the bending, not about a minimum. y=ex is convex but has no minimum point.

    Flip it: Concave is the opposite: it bends downwards.

    See also: concave, second derivative, point of inflection

    Cosecant (cosec) Trigonometry Year 2

    1 divided by the sine of an angle. This is the reciprocal of sine.

    Examples:cosecx=1sinx. For example cosec(30°)=11/2=2.The graph has vertical asymptotes where sinx=0, at x=0°, 180°, 360° and so on. It never takes a value strictly between −1 and 1 (its values are 1 or more, or −1 or less).

    Watch out: Write cosec (the form used in this book; some calculators and books write csc). It is not the inverse sine sin−1.

    See also: Sine (sin), Secant (sec), Cotangent (cot), Identity 1 + cot² = cosec²

    Cosine (cos) Trigonometry Year 1

    In a right-angled triangle, the adjacent side divided by the hypotenuse. For any angle, the x-coordinate of the matching point on the unit circle.

    Examples:A right-angled triangle has a 60° angle and hypotenuse 8. The side next to the angle is 8 × cos 60° = 4, because cos(60°)=12.On the Unit circle, the point at 120° has x-coordinate cos(120°)=−12. Cosine is negative for angles between 90° and 270°.

    Watch out: The graph of cosine is the graph of Sine (sin) moved 90° to the left, so cosx=sin(x+90°). Sine starts at 0 and cosine starts at 1. Do not mix them up.

    Flip it: The reverse question is "which angle has this cosine?". That is Inverse cosine (arccos, cos−¹).

    See also: Sine (sin), Tangent (tan), the trigonometric function, Unit circle, Secant (sec), Inverse cosine (arccos, cos−¹)

    Cosine rule Trigonometry Year 1

    A rule that links the three sides of a triangle to one of its angles. It is Pythagoras' theorem with an extra term added.

    Examples:In triangle ABC, with side a opposite angle A: a2=b2+c2−2bccosATo find an angle, rearrange it: cosA=b2+c2−a22bc. With sides 5, 6 and 7 and A opposite the side 7: cosA=25+36−4960=15, so A = 78.5° to 1 decimal place.

    Watch out: The angle in the formula is the one between sides b and c, and the side on the left is the one opposite that angle. If A = 90°, then cos A = 0 and the rule becomes Pythagoras' theorem.

    Flip it: Use it when you know two sides and the angle between them, or all three sides. Use the Sine rule when you have a matching side and angle.

    See also: Sine rule, Area of a triangle, ½ab sin C

    Cotangent (cot) Trigonometry Year 2

    1 divided by the tangent of an angle. It also equals cosine divided by sine.

    Examples:cotx=1tanx=cosxsinx. For example cot(45°)=1.The graph has period 180° and vertical asymptotes where sinx=0.

    Watch out: It is not the inverse tangent tan−1. Between asymptotes its graph falls from left to right, the opposite of tan, which rises.

    See also: Tangent (tan), the trigonometric function, Secant (sec), Cosecant (cosec), Identity 1 + cot² = cosec²

    counterexample Proof Year 1

    One example that makes a statement false. One such example is enough to disprove the statement.

    Examples:Claim: "n2+n+41 is prime for every integer n from 0 upwards."It works for n = 0, 1, 2 and many more.But for n=40, n2+n+41=1681=412. This is not prime, so the claim is false.

    Watch out: Show the working that proves your example really breaks the statement. Many examples that work prove nothing.

    Flip it: A counterexample can only disprove a statement. To prove a statement you need a proof.

    See also: proof, conjecture, statement

    cubic Algebra and functions Year 1

    A polynomial of degree 3, or its graph. The highest power of x is 3.

    Examples:y=x3−3x is a cubic. It crosses the x-axis at −3, 0 and 3.If the coefficient of x3 is positive, the graph rises from left to right overall. If it is negative, the graph falls.

    Watch out: A cubic has at least one real root and at most three.

    See also: polynomial, quartic, degree (of a polynomial), factor theorem

    D

    decreasing function Differentiation Year 1

    A function whose graph never goes up as you move to the right along an interval. Its derivative is negative or zero there.

    Example: For y=x2−4x, dydx=2x−4. This is zero or negative when x≤2. So the function is decreasing for x≤2.

    Watch out: Solve dydx≤0 as an inequality, and write the answer as x-values. It is the sign of the gradient that matters, not whether y itself is negative.

    Flip it: An increasing function is the opposite: its derivative is positive or zero.

    See also: increasing function, stationary point, derivative

    Decreasing sequence Sequences and series Year 2

    A sequence in which every term is smaller than the one before it.

    Example: 20, 17, 14, 11 … is decreasing. 1, 12, 14 … is also decreasing.

    Watch out: A sequence of negative numbers can be decreasing even though the numbers get larger if you ignore the minus signs: −1,−3,−9 …

    Flip it: In an increasing sequence every term is bigger than the one before.

    See also: Increasing sequence

    definite integral Integration Year 1

    An integral with a lower limit and an upper limit. Its value is a number: the antiderivative at the upper limit minus the antiderivative at the lower limit.

    Example: The antiderivative of 2x is x2. So ∫132xdx=32−12=8.

    Watch out: Work out upper minus lower, not the other way round. Do not write +c. A definite integral can be negative or zero. It equals the area only when the curve is above the x-axis.

    Flip it: An indefinite integral has no limits and gives a function.

    See also: indefinite integral, limits of integration, area under a curve, fundamental theorem of calculus

    degree (of a polynomial) Algebra and functions Year 1

    The highest power of x in a polynomial.

    Examples:3x4−2x2+1 has degree 4.A quadratic has degree 2. A cubic has degree 3.

    Watch out: The degree of a polynomial is not the degree of an angle. It is a power, not a coefficient: 7x2 has degree 2, not 7.

    See also: polynomial, cubic, quartic, coefficient

    derivative Differentiation Year 1

    A function that gives the gradient of a curve at every point. You find it by differentiating.

    Example: If y=x2, the derivative is dydx=2x, read as "dy by dx equals 2x". At x=3 the gradient is 6. Another way to write it: if f(x)=x2, then f′(x) = 2x, read as "f prime of x equals 2x".

    Watch out: The derivative is a function. The gradient at one point is a single value of it. Find that value by putting the x-value into the derivative, not into the original function.

    Flip it: Integration reverses differentiation.

    See also: differentiate, gradient of a curve, second derivative, integral

    Taught in: Integration as reverse differentiation

    derivative of x to the n Differentiation Year 1

    The rule that the derivative of x to the power n is n times x to the power of (n minus 1).

    Examples:ddx(x5)=5x4.Rewrite roots and fractions as powers first. x=x1/2, so its derivative is 1/2×x−1/2. 1x2=x−2, so its derivative is −2x−3.A constant multiple stays: the derivative of 4x3 is 12x2. A constant on its own gives 0.

    Watch out: Rewrite the term as a power of x before you differentiate. 1x2 does not differentiate to 12x. The rule works for every number n, including negatives and fractions. Remember that x is x1, so its derivative is 1.

    Flip it: Integration adds 1 to the power and divides by the new power. See integral of x to the n.

    See also: differentiation from first principles, differentiate, integral of x to the n

    Taught in: Integration as reverse differentiation

    Diameter Coordinate geometry Year 1

    A straight line across a circle that passes through the centre. Its length is twice the radius.

    Examples:A diameter has end points (1, 2) and (7, 10).The centre is the midpoint: (4, 6). The length is 62+82=10, so the radius is 5.The circle is (x−4)2+(y−6)2=25.

    Watch out: The diameter is the length across, 2r. The radius is half of it.

    Flip it: The midpoint of a diameter is the centre.

    See also: Radius, Centre of a circle, Chord, Angle in a semicircle

    differential equation Integration Year 2

    An equation that contains a derivative. Solving it means finding the function that satisfies it.

    Examples:dydx=3x2 is a differential equation. Integrating gives y=x3+c.It is first order, because it contains only the first derivative.

    Watch out: Check a solution by differentiating it and putting it back in the equation.

    Flip it: Differentiating the solution gets you back to the differential equation.

    See also: general solution, particular solution, separable differential equation, initial condition

    differentiate Differentiation Year 1

    To find the derivative of a function.

    Example: Differentiate y=3x2−5x+1. Differentiate each term: dydx=6x−5. The constant 1 gives 0.

    Watch out: "Differentiate with respect to x" means treat x as the variable. Every other letter is a constant.

    Flip it: Integrate the derivative and you get back to the function, plus a constant.

    See also: derivative, derivative of x to the n, integrate

    Taught in: Integration as reverse differentiation

    differentiation from first principles Differentiation Year 1

    Finding the derivative directly from its definition: the limit of the gradient of a chord as the two points of the chord come together.

    Examples:The definition is f′(x) = limh→0f(x+h)−f(x)h.For f(x)=x2: (x+h)2−x2h=2xh+h2h=2x+h.As h gets closer to 0, 2x+h gets closer to 2x. So f′(x) = 2x.

    Watch out: Simplify the fraction fully before letting h get close to 0. While you are dividing by h, h is not 0. Keep writing limh→0 on each line until you take the limit. For sin x and cos x (Year 2), you also need the small-angle approximations.

    Flip it: The rule for xn is a shortcut. It comes from using first principles on xn. See derivative of x to the n.

    See also: chord of a curve, limit, derivative, derivative of x to the n

    Direction of a vector Vectors Year 1

    The way a vector points, usually given as the angle it makes with the positive x-axis, measured anticlockwise.

    Examples:(34): tanθ=43, so θ=53.1° to 1 decimal place.(−3−4) points into the lower left. The calculator gives 53.1°. The direction is 180°+53.1°=233.1°.

    Watch out: Sketch the vector before you use inverse tangent. The calculator cannot tell which quadrant the vector is in.

    Flip it: Given a magnitude and a direction, the components are |a|cosθ across and |a|sinθ up.

    See also: Component, Magnitude

    Discontinuity Numerical methods Year 2

    A point where the graph of a function has a break: a gap, a jump or an asymptote.

    Examples:f(x)=1x−1 has a discontinuity at x=1, where it has a vertical asymptote.f(0)=−1 and f(2)=1, so f changes sign between 0 and 2. But there is no root there: the sign change happens at the asymptote.

    Watch out: A sign change across a discontinuity does not mean there is a root. This is the most common way the Change of sign method fails: always check that the function is continuous on the interval.

    See also: Continuous function, Change of sign

    discriminant Algebra and functions Year 1

    For a quadratic with coefficients a, b and c, the number b squared minus 4ac. Its sign tells you how many real roots there are.

    Examples:For x2+5x+4, the discriminant is 52−4×1×4=9. It is positive, so there are two different real roots.Positive: two different real roots. Zero: one repeated root. Negative: no real roots.

    Watch out: The discriminant is not the answer to the equation. It only tells you how many roots there are.

    Flip it: To test whether a line meets a curve, substitute to get a quadratic. A discriminant of 0 means the line is a tangent.

    See also: quadratic, quadratic formula, root (of an equation or function), repeated root

    Displacement Vectors Year 1

    The vector from one position to another: the straight-line move, with its direction.

    Example: From A (1, 2) to B (4, 6) the displacement is (34). Its magnitude is 5, which is the distance in a straight line.

    Watch out: Displacement is not the distance travelled. Walk 3 m east and then 3 m west: you travelled 6 m, but your displacement is the Zero vector.

    See also: Position vector, Vector

    Distance between two points Coordinate geometry Year 1

    The length of the straight line between two points. It comes from Pythagoras’ theorem on the horizontal and vertical steps between them.

    Examples:From (1, 1) to (5, 4): across 4 and up 3, so d=42+32=25=5.The general formula is d=(x2−x1)2+(y2−y1)2.

    Watch out: Square each step before you add. The square of a negative step is positive, so the order of the points does not matter. The distance is never negative.

    See also: Line segment, Midpoint, Radius

    Distance in three dimensions Vectors Year 2

    The distance between two points in space. It is the square root of the sum of the squares of the differences in x, y and z.

    Examples:d=(x2−x1)2+(y2−y1)2+(z2−z1)2.From (1, 2, 3) to (4, 6, 15): the differences are 3, 4 and 12, so d=9+16+144=169=13.

    Watch out: Square each difference before you add. The distance is the magnitude of the vector between the points.

    Flip it: In a box with sides a, b and c, the longest diagonal is a2+b2+c2.

    See also: Magnitude, Three-dimensional axes, Displacement

    Divergence Numerical methods Year 2

    When the values given by an iteration do not settle on one number. They may move away from the root, or keep jumping from value to value.

    Examples:xn+1=xn22 from x0=2.2 gives 2.42, 2.93, 4.29, 9.2 … The values grow without limit.The number 2 satisfies 2=222, so it is a fixed point. But the iteration moves away from it, so it never finds it.

    Watch out: Divergence happens when the gradient of g at the fixed point is bigger than 1 or less than −1. If an iteration diverges, try another rearrangement of the equation.

    Flip it: The opposite is Convergence.

    See also: Convergence, Fixed point, Staircase diagram, Cobweb diagram

    Divergent Sequences and series Year 2

    A sequence or series that does not settle on one fixed value. It may grow without limit or keep jumping about.

    Examples:2, 4, 8, 16 … grows without limit.1, −1, 1, −1 … stays small but never settles, so it is divergent too.The series 1+2+4+8 … is divergent.

    Watch out: Divergent does not always mean "goes to infinity". A sequence that jumps between two values also diverges.

    Flip it: A sequence or series that settles is Convergent.

    See also: Convergent, Oscillating sequence

    domain Algebra and functions Year 2

    The set of input values a function is allowed to take.

    Examples:f(x)=x−1 has domain x≥1.f(x)=1x has domain x≠0."f(x)=x2, x≥0" has the domain x≥0, set by the question.

    Watch out: The domain is a set of x-values, not y-values. If the question gives no domain, use every real number that does not break the rule.

    Flip it: The domain of f is the range of the inverse function f−1.

    See also: range (of a function), function, inverse function, real number (ℝ)

    Double-angle formulae Trigonometry Year 2

    Formulae that give the sine, cosine or tangent of twice an angle in terms of the angle itself.

    Examples:sin2A=2sinAcosAcos2A=cos2A−sin2A=2cos2A−1=1−2sin2Atan2A=2tanA1−tan2AIf cosA=35 then cos2A=2×925−1=−725.

    Watch out: sin2A is not 2sinA. There are three forms of cos2A: choose the form that contains only the function you are given.

    Flip it: Rearranged, they give cos2A=1+cos2A2. Integration uses this to integrate cos2A.

    See also: Addition formulae (compound angle formulae), R-form (harmonic form)

    E

    element of (∈) Algebra and functions Year 1

    The sign ∈ means "is a member of". Writing x ∈ A says that x is in the set A.

    Examples:If A is the set {1, 2, 3}, then 3∈A.x∈ℝ says that x is a real number.

    Watch out: The sign ∈ relates a member to a set. It does not compare two numbers.

    See also: set notation, real number (ℝ), domain

    Eliminate the parameter Coordinate geometry Year 2

    Remove the parameter from a pair of parametric equations to get one equation in x and y.

    Examples:Make t the subject of one equation and substitute it into the other. Try x=2t+1, y=t2: t=x−12, so y=(x−1)24.For equations with sin t and cos t, use sin2t+cos2t=1. From x=3cost, y=3sint: x2+y2=9(cos2t+sin2t)=9.

    Watch out: Square and substitute with care. Squaring can add values that the original curve does not have, so check the range of x and y.

    See also: Parametric equations, Cartesian equation, Parameter

    Equation of a circle Coordinate geometry Year 1

    The equation (x − a)² + (y − b)² = r² describes the circle with centre (a, b) and radius r. Read it as "x minus a, squared, plus y minus b, squared, equals r squared".

    Examples:Centre (2, 1), radius 2: (x−2)2+(y−1)2=4.Read off (x+1)2+(y−4)2=9: centre (-1, 4), radius 3.With centre at the origin it is x2+y2=r2.

    Watch out: The signs inside the brackets are opposite to the centre’s coordinates. The right side is r2, so take a square root to get the radius.

    Flip it: To write the equation without brackets, expand them. That gives the general form.

    See also: General form of a circle, Centre of a circle, Radius

    Equation of a straight line, y = mx + c Coordinate geometry Year 1

    An equation in x and y whose graph is a straight line. In the form y = mx + c, the number m is the gradient and c is where the line crosses the y-axis.

    Examples:y=2x+1 has gradient 2 and crosses the y-axis at 1.Rearrange 3y−6x=12: divide by 3 to get y−2x=4, so y=2x+4. The gradient is 2 and c is 4.

    Watch out: The equation must be in the form y=mx+c before you read off m and c. In 3y=6x+12, the gradient is 2, not 6.

    Flip it: Give the gradient and the y-intercept and the line is fixed: write them into y=mx+c.

    See also: Gradient, y-intercept, Point-gradient form, y - y1 = m(x - x1), General form of a line, ax + by + c = 0

    even number Proof Year 1

    An integer that is a multiple of 2. Written with a letter, an even number is 2n, where n is an integer.

    Examples:The even numbers: −4, −2, 0, 2, 4, 6.In a proof, call an even number 2n. Two different even numbers are 2a and 2b.

    Watch out: Zero is even. Negative integers can be even too, such as −6.

    Flip it: An integer that is not even is odd number.

    See also: odd number, integer, consecutive integers, proof by deduction

    Exact value Trigonometry Year 1

    A sine, cosine or tangent value written with fractions and surds, not as a rounded decimal.

    Examples:sin(30°)=12, sin(45°)=22, sin(60°)=32.cos(30°)=32, cos(45°)=22, cos(60°)=12.tan(30°)=13, tan(45°)=1, tan(60°)=3.

    Watch out: Do not give a rounded calculator answer when the question says "exact". To rebuild these values, draw half of an equilateral triangle with side 2 (for 30° and 60°). Draw a right-angled triangle with two sides of 1 (for 45°).

    Flip it: Use the CAST diagram and symmetry to get exact values of larger angles, such as sin(150°)=12.

    See also: CAST diagram, Unit circle

    Exponential decay Exponentials and logs Year 1

    A quantity is multiplied by the same number, between 0 and 1, in every equal time step. It falls quickly at first and then more slowly.

    Examples:A car is worth 15000 pounds and loses 20% of its value each year: V=15000×0.8t. After 2 years, V=15000×0.64=9600 pounds.y=A×bx with 0<b<1, or y=Ae−kx with k>0, are both exponential decay.

    Watch out: The quantity never reaches 0 in this model: the graph gets closer and closer to the x-axis. A fall of 20% multiplies by 0.8, not by 0.2.

    Flip it: If the factor is bigger than 1, the quantity grows: Exponential growth.

    See also: Exponential growth, Growth factor (multiplier), Half-life, Continuous growth model (rate proportional to size)

    Exponential equation Exponentials and logs Year 1

    An equation in which the unknown is in the power, usually solved by taking logarithms of both sides.

    Examples:Solve 2x=10. Take logarithms of both sides: xlog2=log10. So x=log10log2=3.32 to 3 significant figures.Solve e2x−5ex+6=0. Let u=ex. Then u2−5u+6=0, so u=2 or u=3. So x=ln2 or x=ln3.

    Watch out: Use the power law to take the unknown out of the power. Do not take the logarithm of each term separately. For ex=−2, there is no solution, because ex is always positive.

    See also: Power law of logarithms, Logarithm and exponential are inverses, Change of base

    Exponential function Exponentials and logs Year 1

    A function such as a to the power x, where the unknown x is in the power. The base a is a positive number other than 1.

    Examples:y=2x: the values for x=0,1,2,3 are 1, 2, 4, 8. The graph passes through (0, 1) and goes up faster and faster.y=(12)x: the values are 1, 12, 14, 18. The graph passes through (0, 1) and falls towards 0.

    Watch out: An exponential function is not the same as y=x2. In x2 the unknown is the base; in 2x the unknown is the power. The graph of y=ax is always above the x-axis and gets closer and closer to the line y=0 (an asymptote) but never reaches it.

    Flip it: The inverse of an exponential function is a Logarithm (log): 2x=8 has the answer x=log28=3.

    See also: Base, Exponential growth, Exponential decay, Natural exponential function (e^x), Logarithm (log)

    Exponential growth Exponentials and logs Year 1

    A quantity is multiplied by the same number, bigger than 1, in every equal time step. The bigger it gets, the faster it rises.

    Examples:A population starts at 100 and doubles every hour: N=100×2t, with t in hours. After 3 hours, N=100×8=800.y=A×bx with b>1, or y=Aekx with k>0, are both exponential growth.

    Watch out: Exponential growth is not the same as growing by a fixed amount each time (that is linear, a straight line). A growth of 5% a year multiplies by 1.05, not 0.05.

    Flip it: If the factor is between 0 and 1, the quantity falls: Exponential decay.

    See also: Exponential decay, Growth factor (multiplier), Exponential model, Continuous growth model (rate proportional to size)

    Exponential model Exponentials and logs Year 1

    A formula such as y = A times b to the power x, or A e to the power kx. It describes something that changes by the same percentage in each equal step.

    Examples:A bank account of 500 pounds earns 4% a year: S=500×1.04t. After 10 years, S=500×1.0410=740.12 pounds.A is the starting value: it is the value when t=0.

    Watch out: A model works only if its assumptions are true. Real populations run out of room and food, and real decay can speed up or slow down, so exponential growth cannot go on for ever. State the limits: for example "only for a short time" or "only for small populations".

    See also: Exponential growth, Exponential decay, Growth factor (multiplier), Semi-log graph

    F

    factor theorem Algebra and functions Year 1

    The expression (x minus a) is a factor of the polynomial f(x) exactly when f(a) equals 0.

    Examples:f(x)=x3+2x2−5x−6. f(2)=8+8−10−6=0, so (x−2) is a factor.Dividing gives f(x)=(x−2)(x+1)(x+3).

    Watch out: To find a first factor, try values of a that divide the constant term: for −6, try ±1, ±2, ±3 and ±6. This works when the coefficient of the highest power is 1.

    Flip it: If you know the roots of a polynomial, you know its factors.

    See also: remainder theorem, root (of an equation or function), polynomial division, cubic

    Factorial, n! Sequences and series Year 1

    The product of all the whole numbers from n down to 1, written n! and read "n factorial". By agreement, 0! is 1.

    Examples:5!=5×4×3×2×1=120.Cancel before you multiply: 7!5!=7×6=42.

    Watch out: (2n)! is not 2×n!. Factorials grow very fast: 10!=3628800.

    Flip it: n! counts the ways to put n different things in a line.

    See also: nCr (binomial coefficient), Pascal’s triangle

    family of solution curves Integration Year 2

    The set of curves given by a general solution, one curve for each value of the constant.

    Example: For dydx=2x, the curves y=x2−2, y=x2 and y=x2+2 are in the family y=x2+c. Each has gradient 2x at the same x-value.

    Watch out: A given point fits only one curve of the family. That curve is the particular solution.

    See also: general solution, particular solution, constant of integration

    Fixed point Numerical methods Year 2

    A value x for which g(x) = x, so that putting it into an iterative formula gives the same value back.

    Examples:For g(x)=cosx, the fixed point is where cosx=x. That is x=0.739 to 3 decimal places.On a graph, it is where y=g(x) crosses the line y=x. The root you want is the x-coordinate of that crossing.

    Watch out: A fixed point exists whether or not the iteration finds it. An iteration finds the fixed point only if the iteration converges (see Convergence).

    Flip it: If an iteration converges, the limit L is a fixed point: L=g(L).

    See also: Iterative formula, Convergence, Staircase diagram, Cobweb diagram

    fractional index Algebra and functions Year 1

    An index that is a fraction. The bottom of the fraction is the root and the top is the power.

    Examples:x12=x and x13=x3.2723=(273)2=32=9.

    Watch out: Take the root first, then the power. The numbers stay small. Roots of negative numbers are not real when the root is even.

    See also: index (power), laws of indices, negative index, surd

    function Algebra and functions Year 1

    A rule that takes each allowed input and gives exactly one output. Year 1 needs the notation f(x). Mapping, domain, range, composite functions and inverse functions come in Year 2.

    Examples:f(x)=2x+1. The input 3 gives the output f(3)=7.Another way to write it: f:x↦2x+1, read "f maps x to 2x + 1".

    Watch out: The notation f(x) does not mean f times x. And y=±x is not a function, because one input gives two outputs.

    Flip it: Some functions can be undone. See inverse function.

    See also: mapping, domain, range (of a function), inverse function, composite function

    fundamental theorem of calculus Integration Year 1

    Differentiation and integration reverse each other. The definite integral of f from a to b equals F(b) minus F(a), where F is any antiderivative of f.

    Examples:∫03x2dx=333−033=9.The other half of the theorem: if A(x) is the area under the graph of f from a to x, then the derivative of A(x) is f(x).

    Watch out: The theorem is why you can find an area by using an antiderivative. Any antiderivative works, because the constant cancels in F(b) minus F(a).

    See also: definite integral, antiderivative, integration as the limit of a sum

    G

    General form of a circle Coordinate geometry Year 1

    The expanded equation of a circle, in which x² and y² both have coefficient 1 and there are terms in x and y, such as x² + y² − 4x − 2y − 4 = 0.

    Examples:Complete the square on x2+y2−4x−2y−4=0.(x−2)2−4+(y−1)2−1−4=0, so (x−2)2+(y−1)2=9.The centre is (2, 1) and the radius is 3.Shortcut for x2+y2+2gx+2fy+c=0: the centre is (−g,−f) and r2=g2+f2−c.

    Watch out: After completing the square, check that the right side is positive. If it is 0 the graph is one point. If it is negative there is no graph. Make the coefficients of x2 and y2 equal to 1 first: divide through if they are not.

    Flip it: Expanding (x−a)2+(y−b)2=r2 and moving everything to one side gives the general form.

    See also: Equation of a circle, Centre of a circle, Radius

    General form of a line, ax + by + c = 0 Coordinate geometry Year 1

    A way of writing a line with everything on one side and 0 on the other: ax + by + c = 0. Exam questions usually ask for integers a, b and c.

    Examples:y=23x+1 becomes 3y=2x+3, then 2x−3y+3=0.To read the gradient, rearrange back: by=−ax−c, so m=−ab.

    Watch out: In this form, c is not the y-intercept. The y-intercept is −cb. Clear any fractions before you give the final answer.

    See also: Equation of a straight line, y = mx + c, Point-gradient form, y - y1 = m(x - x1)

    general solution Integration Year 2

    A solution of a differential equation that still contains an arbitrary constant. It describes a whole family of curves.

    Example: The general solution of dydx=2x is y=x2+c. The general solution of dydx=2y is y=Ae2x.

    Watch out: Keep the constant. A first-order equation has one constant. Replace the constant with a number only when you are given extra information (an initial condition).

    Flip it: An initial condition fixes the constant and gives a particular solution.

    See also: particular solution, family of solution curves, constant of integration

    Geometric sequence Sequences and series Year 2

    A sequence in which you multiply by the same number each time to get the next term.

    Examples:3, 6, 12, 24 … multiplies by 2 each time.The nth term is un=arn−1, where a is the first term and r is the common ratio. Here un=3×2n−1, so u4=3×8=24.

    Watch out: The power is n−1, not n. It is only r that is raised to the power: arn−1 is not (ar)n−1.

    Flip it: A sequence is geometric if each term divided by the one before gives the same number.

    See also: Common ratio, Geometric series

    Geometric series Sequences and series Year 2

    The sum of the terms of a geometric sequence.

    Examples:The sum of the first n terms is Sn=a(1−rn)1−r, which equals a(rn−1)r−1.3+6+12+24+48: a=3, r=2, n=5, so S5=3(25−1)2−1=93.

    Watch out: The formula fails when r=1, because it divides by 0. Then every term is a, so Sn=na. Use the form with rn−1 on top when r>1: it keeps the numbers positive.

    Flip it: Why it works: take Sn and rSn, subtract, and nearly every term cancels.

    See also: Geometric sequence, Sum to infinity, Sum of the first n terms, S_n

    global maximum and minimum Differentiation Year 1

    The greatest and the least value a function takes on a given interval. Each one is at a stationary point or at an end of the interval.

    Example: For y=x2−4x with 0≤x≤5: the stationary point (2, -4) gives the least value. At the ends, y is 0 and 5. So the greatest value is 5, at x=5.

    Watch out: A local maximum is not always the global maximum. Compare the y-values at every stationary point and both ends of the interval.

    See also: maximum point, minimum point, optimisation

    Gradient Coordinate geometry Year 1

    How steep a line is: the change in y divided by the change in x, between any two points on the line.

    Examples:The line through (1, 1) and (3, 5) has m=5−13−1=42=2. It goes up 2 for every 1 across.The general formula is m=y2−y1x2−x1.

    Watch out: Take the coordinates in the same order on the top and the bottom. Mixing the order flips the sign. A line that goes down to the right has a negative gradient. A horizontal line has gradient 0. A vertical line has no gradient, because its change in x is 0 and you cannot divide by 0. On a curve the gradient changes from point to point. The gradient of a curve at a point means the gradient of the Tangent there.

    Flip it: If you know the gradient and one point, you can find every other point: go across 1 and up by the gradient, again and again.

    See also: Equation of a straight line, y = mx + c, Parallel lines, Perpendicular, Angle of inclination

    Taught in: Integration as reverse differentiation

    gradient of a curve Differentiation Year 1

    How steep a curve is at one point. It equals the gradient of the tangent to the curve at that point.

    Example: On y=x2, the gradient at x=3 is 6. The tangent at (3, 9) rises 6 units for every 1 unit across.

    Watch out: A curve has a different gradient at different points, so always say which point. A straight line has the same gradient everywhere.

    Flip it: Differentiation finds the gradient at every point at once. Integration goes back from the gradient to the curve.

    See also: derivative, tangent to a curve, chord of a curve

    Graph of a logarithm Exponentials and logs Year 1

    The graph of y = log to the base a of x. It passes through (1, 0), exists only for x greater than 0 and has the y-axis as an asymptote.

    Examples:y=log2x passes through (1, 0), (2, 1), (4, 2) and (8, 3). It rises slowly. For 0<x<1 it is negative.The graph of y=lnx has the same shape, passing through (1, 0) and (e, 1).

    Watch out: The graph never touches the y-axis, and no part of it lies to the left of the y-axis. Do not draw it curving back to meet the y-axis or crossing it: as x gets close to 0 the graph keeps falling, but never reaches the axis.

    Flip it: It is the reflection of y=ax in the line y=x: the point (p,q) on one becomes (q,p) on the other.

    See also: Logarithm (log), Natural logarithm (ln), Logarithm and exponential are inverses, Exponential function

    Growth factor (multiplier) Exponentials and logs Year 1

    The number you multiply by in each time step. It is greater than 1 for growth and between 0 and 1 for decay.

    Examples:A rise of 5% each year has growth factor 1+5100=1.05.A fall of 20% each year has factor 1−20100=0.8.

    Watch out: The factor is not the percentage. A 5% rise is 1.05, not 0.05. In y=A×bx the growth factor is b.

    See also: Exponential growth, Exponential decay, Exponential model

    H

    Half-life Exponentials and logs Year 1

    The time it takes for a decaying quantity to fall to half of what it was at the start of that time.

    Examples:A substance has half-life 2 days. From 8 g, it falls to 4 g after 2 days, then to 2 g after 4 days, then to 1 g after 6 days.The model is m=8×(12)t/2, with t in days.

    Watch out: The half-life is the same wherever you start. From 4 g, it takes 2 days to reach 2 g, as it took 2 days to go from 8 g to 4 g. Only exponential decay behaves like this.

    Flip it: For growth, the matching idea is the doubling time: how long a growing quantity takes to double.

    See also: Exponential decay, Exponential model

    hence Proof Year 1

    A command word: use the result from the previous part of the question to answer the next part.

    Examples:(a) Factorise x2−5x+6. (b) Hence solve x2−5x+6=0.Use the factorised form from part (a).

    Watch out: If a question says "hence", a method that ignores the previous part may score no marks. "Hence or otherwise" lets you use any valid method.

    See also: show that, therefore (∴)

    I

    i and j notation Vectors Year 1

    A way of writing vectors using two special vectors: i, which is 1 across, and j, which is 1 up. Every two-dimensional vector is a number of i plus a number of j.

    Examples:i is (10) and j is (01).(3−2) = 3i − 2j.

    Watch out: Here i is a vector, not the square root of −1 and not a counting number. The letters are written in bold in print. Do not drop the letter: write 3i − 2j, not 3 − 2.

    See also: Column vector, Unit vector, i, j and k notation

    i, j and k notation Vectors Year 2

    A way of writing three-dimensional vectors using three unit vectors at right angles: i along the x-axis, j along the y-axis and k along the z-axis.

    Examples:2i−3j+5k = (2−35).Its magnitude is 22+(−3)2+52=38.

    Watch out: Include every letter, and write 0 if a component is missing. 3i+2k has a zero j-component: it is (302).

    See also: i and j notation, Three-dimensional axes, Magnitude

    identity (≡) Proof Year 1

    The sign ≡ means that two expressions are equal for every value of the letters. An equation is true only for some values. Read ≡ as "is identical to".

    Examples:(x+1)2≡x2+2x+1 is true for every x.x2=4 is an equation. It is true only for x=2 and x=−2.

    Watch out: Many questions and answers use = where ≡ would be exact. Read the context: "for all x" means identity.

    See also: proof by deduction, show that

    Identity 1 + cot² = cosec² Trigonometry Year 2

    One plus cotangent squared of an angle equals cosecant squared of that angle.

    Examples:1+cot2θ=cosec2θDivide every term of sin2θ+cos2θ=1 by sin2θ to get it.

    Watch out: It does not hold where sinθ=0, because cot and cosec do not exist there.

    See also: Pythagorean identity, sin² + cos² = 1, Identity 1 + tan² = sec², Cosecant (cosec), Cotangent (cot)

    Identity 1 + tan² = sec² Trigonometry Year 2

    One plus tangent squared of an angle equals secant squared of that angle.

    Examples:1+tan2θ=sec2θDivide every term of sin2θ+cos2θ=1 by cos2θ to get it. Use it to change an equation with several trigonometric functions into one with only tan or only sec.

    Watch out: It does not hold where cosθ=0, because sec and tan do not exist there. Writing sec2θ means (secθ)2.

    See also: Pythagorean identity, sin² + cos² = 1, Identity 1 + cot² = cosec², Secant (sec), Tangent (tan), the trigonometric function

    if and only if (⇔) Proof Year 1

    The sign for "each statement implies the other", so the two statements are either both true or both false.

    Examples:2x+1=7⇔x=3. Each side follows from the other.Read it as "2x + 1 = 7 if and only if x = 3".

    Watch out: Squaring cannot be reversed, so it does not give ⇔. x=3⇒x2=9, but x2=9 does not give x=3 on its own. Check each step can be reversed before you write ⇔.

    Flip it: To prove "A if and only if B", prove two things: A ⇒ B and B ⇒ A.

    See also: implies (⇒), converse

    implicit differentiation Differentiation Year 2

    Finding dy by dx when x and y are mixed together in one equation, by differentiating every term with respect to x.

    Examples:For x2+y2=25, differentiate each term with respect to x.The derivative of y2 is 2y×dydx by the chain rule. So 2x+2y×dydx=0, which gives dydx=−xy.At (3, 4) the gradient is −3/4.

    Watch out: Every term in y gets a factor of dydx. A term such as xy needs the product rule. The answer usually has both x and y in it, so you need both coordinates to find a gradient.

    See also: chain rule, product rule, tangent to a curve, parametric differentiation

    implies (⇒) Proof Year 1

    The sign for "if A is true, then B is true". Read A ⇒ B as "A implies B".

    Examples:x=3⇒x2=9 is true: if x is 3, then x2 is 9.The sign ⇐ points the other way. A⇐B is read "A is implied by B".

    Watch out: A ⇒ B does not mean B ⇒ A. Here x2=9 does not imply x=3, because x could be −3.

    Flip it: When both directions hold, use if and only if (⇔).

    See also: if and only if (⇔), converse, therefore (∴)

    improper algebraic fraction Algebra and functions Year 2

    An algebraic fraction where the degree of the top is the same as or greater than the degree of the bottom.

    Examples:x2+1x−1 is improper. Divide first: x2+1x−1=x+1+2x−1.The same idea works with numbers: 73=2+13.

    Watch out: Divide before you try partial fractions. Partial fractions on an improper fraction do not work without a polynomial part.

    See also: partial fractions, polynomial division, algebraic fraction

    increasing function Differentiation Year 1

    A function whose graph never goes down as you move to the right along an interval. Its derivative is positive or zero there.

    Example: For y=x2−4x, dydx=2x−4. This is zero or positive when x≥2. So the function is increasing for x≥2.

    Watch out: Solve dydx≥0 as an inequality. The answer is a range of x-values, not a range of y-values. Some books use a strict sign (> 0) for "strictly increasing".

    Flip it: A decreasing function is the opposite: its derivative is negative or zero.

    See also: decreasing function, stationary point, derivative

    Increasing sequence Sequences and series Year 2

    A sequence in which every term is bigger than the one before it.

    Example: 2, 5, 8, 11 … is increasing. un=nn+1 gives 12,23,34 …, which is also increasing.

    Watch out: Increasing does not mean the terms go on to infinity. The second example never gets above 1. To prove a sequence is increasing, show that un+1−un>0 for every n.

    Flip it: In a decreasing sequence every term is smaller than the one before.

    See also: Decreasing sequence, Convergent

    indefinite integral Integration Year 1

    An integral with no limits. The answer is a function plus a constant c.

    Example: ∫(6x2+2x)dx=2x3+x2+c.

    Watch out: Always add the constant c. The answer is not a number, so you cannot find a value without more information.

    Flip it: A definite integral has limits and gives a number.

    See also: definite integral, constant of integration, integrate

    index (power) Algebra and functions Year 1

    The small raised number in a power. For a whole-number index, it says how many copies of the base to multiply together. The plural is indices.

    Examples:25=2×2×2×2×2=32. Here 2 is the base and 5 is the index.x3 is read "x cubed" or "x to the power 3".

    Watch out: An index applies only to the thing directly in front of it. 2x3 means 2 times x3, but (2x)3=8x3.

    Flip it: A root, such as a cube root, undoes a power: the cube root of x3 is x.

    See also: laws of indices, negative index, fractional index

    Taught in: Integration as reverse differentiation

    inequality Algebra and functions Year 1

    A statement that compares two values using less than, greater than, less than or equal to, or greater than or equal to, instead of an equals sign.

    Examples:2x+1<7 gives x<3.−2x<6 gives x>−3. The inequality sign reverses, because you divided by a negative number.x2−3x+2<0 gives 1<x<2, because the parabola is below the x-axis between its roots 1 and 2.

    Watch out: Multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the sign. Strict signs, < and >, do not include the end value. The signs ≤ and ≥ do.

    Flip it: An inequality usually has a whole range of solutions, shown on a number line or as an interval. An equation usually has separate, individual solutions.

    See also: interval, interval notation, set notation, region (of an inequality), union (∪)

    initial condition Integration Year 2

    A known pair of values, such as y equals 5 when x equals 0, used to find the constant in a general solution.

    Example: The curve has dydx=2x. The condition is y=5 when x=1. From y=x2+c: 5=1+c, so c=4.

    Watch out: The condition may be given as a point the curve passes through. Substitute both values, x and y, into the general solution.

    See also: particular solution, general solution

    integer Proof Year 1

    A number with no fractional part. It can be positive, negative or zero.

    Examples:Integers: −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3.Not integers: 2.5, 12, 2.

    Watch out: Zero is an integer. A fraction such as 63 is an integer, because it equals 2.

    See also: rational number, even number, odd number

    integral Integration Year 1

    The result of integrating a function. Without limits it is a function plus a constant. With limits it is a single number.

    Examples:In symbols, ∫2xdx=x2+c. Read it as "the integral of 2x with respect to x is x squared plus c".The integral of 2x from 1 to 3 is the number 8.

    Watch out: Without limits, always add the constant c. With limits, the answer is a number and has no c.

    Flip it: Differentiating an integral gives back the function you started with.

    See also: integrate, indefinite integral, definite integral, derivative

    Taught in: Integration as reverse differentiation

    integral of f prime over f Integration Year 2

    If the top of a fraction is the derivative of the bottom, its integral is the natural logarithm of the modulus of the bottom, plus c.

    Examples:If the top is f′(x) and the bottom is f(x), then the integral is ln(|f(x)|)+c.∫2xx2+1dx=ln(x2+1)+c. Here the bottom is always positive, so no modulus is needed.∫tan(x)dx=−ln(|cos(x)|)+c, because tan(x)=sin(x)cos(x) and the top is minus the derivative of the bottom.

    Watch out: The top must be the derivative of the bottom, or a constant multiple of it. For a constant multiple, multiply the logarithm by that constant. For ∫1xdx the answer is ln(|x|)+c.

    See also: integration by recognition (reverse chain rule), integral of x to the n

    integral of x to the n Integration Year 1

    The rule: add 1 to the power, then divide by the new power. It works for every n except negative 1.

    Examples:∫xndx=xn+1n+1+c, for n≠−1.∫x4dx=x55+c. And ∫xdx=∫x1/2dx=23x3/2+c.A constant multiple stays outside, and each term is done on its own: ∫(6x2−4)dx=2x3−4x+c.

    Watch out: Rewrite roots and fractions as powers of x first. When n is -1, the rule would divide by 0. That case is ∫1xdx=ln(|x|)+c. Do not forget +c.

    Flip it: Differentiating: multiply by the power, then subtract 1 from the power. See differentiate.

    See also: integrate, constant of integration, integral of f prime over f

    Taught in: Integration as reverse differentiation

    integrand Integration Year 1

    The function that is being integrated: the expression between the integral sign and the dx.

    Example: In ∫02(3x2+1)dx, the integrand is 3x2+1.

    See also: integral, with respect to

    Taught in: Integration as reverse differentiation

    integrate Integration Year 1

    To reverse differentiation: to find a function whose derivative is the function you are given. With limits, the answer is a number, the signed area: parts of the graph above the x-axis count as positive and parts below count as negative.

    Example: Integrate 3x2 with respect to x. The answer is x3+c, because the derivative of x3 is 3x2.

    Watch out: Check an answer by differentiating it. You should get back the function you integrated. Write the dx. It says which variable you are integrating with respect to.

    Flip it: Integration reverses differentiation, except that the constant is lost when you differentiate, so you must add +c back.

    See also: integral, antiderivative, integral of x to the n, differentiate

    Taught in: Integration as reverse differentiation

    integrating with partial fractions Integration Year 2

    Splitting an algebraic fraction into simpler fractions, then integrating each one on its own.

    Examples:1(x−1)(x+2)=13(x−1)−13(x+2).So ∫1(x−1)(x+2)dx=13ln(|x−1|)−13ln(|x+2|)+c.

    Watch out: A fraction with a linear bottom integrates to a natural logarithm: ∫Aax+bdx=Aaln(|ax+b|)+c. A repeated factor such as 1(x−1)2 integrates to −1x−1, not a logarithm. If the highest power of x on the top is the same as or higher than on the bottom, divide first.

    See also: integral of f prime over f, integrate

    integration as the limit of a sum Integration Year 1

    The idea that the area under a curve is the limit of the total area of thin rectangles, as the width of every rectangle shrinks towards zero.

    Examples:Take y=x2 from 0 to 3 and 3 strips of width 1. The strips under the curve add to 0+1+4=5. The strips over the curve add to 1+4+9=14.With more, thinner strips, both totals get closer to the exact area, 9. The integral sign is a stretched S, for "sum".
