    Watch out: A strip gives an estimate, not the exact area. The exact area is the limit as the strips get thinner. On a rising curve, strips whose tops are at the left edge give an underestimate.

    Flip it: You can also find the area under the curve with an antiderivative. See fundamental theorem of calculus.

    See also: area under a curve, definite integral, fundamental theorem of calculus

    integration by parts Integration Year 2

    A method for integrating a product of two functions. Choose u and dv by dx. Then the integral equals u times v, minus the integral of v times du by dx.

    Examples:∫udvdxdx=u×v−∫vdudxdxFor ∫xexdx: let u=x and dvdx=ex. Then dudx=1 and v=ex.The integral is xex−∫exdx=xex−ex+c.For ∫ln(x)dx, let u=ln(x) and dvdx=1. The result is xln(x)−x+c.

    Watch out: Choose u to be the part that gets simpler when you differentiate it, such as x or ln x. Do not lose the minus sign in the formula. For a definite integral, put the limits in the u×v part too. Some integrals need parts twice.

    Flip it: This reverses the product rule.

    See also: integration by substitution, integrate

    integration by recognition (reverse chain rule) Integration Year 2

    Integrating by spotting that the integrand is the result of the chain rule, then adjusting for any constant factor.

    Example: To integrate (2x+1)4, guess (2x+1)5. Its derivative is 10(2x+1)4, which is 10 times too big. So ∫(2x+1)4dx=(2x+1)510+c.

    Watch out: Check by differentiating your answer. For ∫f(ax+b)dx, integrate f and then divide by a. Do not divide by a when the inner function is not linear.

    Flip it: This reverses the chain rule.

    See also: integration by substitution, integral of f prime over f

    integration by substitution Integration Year 2

    A method that replaces part of the integrand with a new variable u, to turn the integral into a simpler one in u.

    Example: For ∫2x(x2+1)3dx, let u=x2+1. Then dudx=2x, so du=2xdx. The integral becomes ∫u3du=u44+c=(x2+1)44+c.

    Watch out: Replace every x, including the dx. Write the answer using x again at the end, unless you have changed the limits. A substitution may be given in the question or you may need to choose it.

    Flip it: This reverses the chain rule.

    See also: changing the limits, integration by recognition (reverse chain rule), integration by parts

    interval Algebra and functions Year 1

    All the numbers between two end values, with or without the end values themselves.

    Examples:The numbers from 1 up to 5, including both ends, form an interval.On a number line a filled circle includes an end value. An open circle leaves it out.

    Watch out: The word "between" is not enough. Say whether each end is included.

    See also: interval notation, inequality, set notation

    interval notation Algebra and functions Year 1

    A short way to write an interval. A square bracket includes an end value. A round bracket leaves it out.

    Examples:[1, 5] means 1≤x≤5.[1, 5) means 1≤x<5.(2, ∞) means x>2.

    Watch out: Infinity is not a number, so it always has a round bracket. Also, (2, 5) looks like coordinates. Check the context.

    See also: interval, inequality, union (∪), set notation

    Inverse cosine (arccos, cos−¹) Trigonometry Year 2

    The function that gives the angle between 0° and 180° (0 and π radians) whose cosine is a given number.

    Examples:Domain: −1≤x≤1. Range: 0≤y≤π.arccos(12)=π3 and arccos(−12)=2×π3.

    Watch out: The range is 0 to π, not −π2 to π2 as for arcsin. A negative number gives an angle bigger than π2.

    Flip it: Its graph is the part of y=cosx between x=0 and x=π, reflected in the line y=x.

    See also: Cosine (cos), Inverse trigonometric functions (sin−¹, arcsin), Inverse sine (arcsin, sin−¹), Inverse tangent (arctan, tan−¹)

    inverse function Algebra and functions Year 2

    The function that undoes f. It sends each output of f back to the input that made it. It is written f⁻¹ and read "f inverse".

    Examples:f(x)=2x+3. To find f−1: write y=2x+3, swap x and y to get x=2y+3, then make y the subject: f−1(x)=x−32.Check: f−1(f(x))=x.The graph of f−1 is the reflection of the graph of f in the line y=x.

    Watch out: The raised −1 is not an index. f−1(x) does not equal 1f(x).

    Flip it: The domain of f−1 is the range of f, and its range is the domain of f.

    See also: one-to-one function, domain, range (of a function), composite function, self-inverse function

    Inverse sine (arcsin, sin−¹) Trigonometry Year 2

    The function that gives the angle between −90° and 90° (that is, −π/2 and π/2 radians) whose sine is a given number.

    Examples:Domain: −1≤x≤1. Range: −π2≤y≤π2.arcsin(12)=π6 and arcsin(−1)=−π2. arcsin2 does not exist, because no angle has sine 2.

    Watch out: The range is restricted, so arcsin(sinx)=x only when x is in that range. For example arcsin(sin(150°))=30°, not 150°.

    Flip it: Its graph is the part of y=sinx between x=−π2 and π2, reflected in the line y=x.

    See also: Sine (sin), Inverse trigonometric functions (sin−¹, arcsin), Inverse cosine (arccos, cos−¹), Inverse tangent (arctan, tan−¹)

    Inverse tangent (arctan, tan−¹) Trigonometry Year 2

    The function that gives the angle between −90° and 90° (not including those two) whose tangent is a given number.

    Examples:Domain: all real numbers. Range: −π2<y<π2.arctan1=π4 and arctan(−1)=−π4. The graph has horizontal asymptotes at y=π2 and y=−π2.

    Watch out: Unlike arcsin and arccos, its domain is every real number, because every number is the tangent of some angle.

    Flip it: Its graph is the part of y=tanx between the asymptotes x=−π2 and π2, reflected in the line y=x.

    See also: Tangent (tan), the trigonometric function, Inverse trigonometric functions (sin−¹, arcsin), Inverse sine (arcsin, sin−¹), Inverse cosine (arccos, cos−¹)

    Inverse trigonometric functions (sin−¹, arcsin) Trigonometry Year 2

    The functions that undo sine, cosine and tangent: they take a ratio and give back the angle.

    Examples:The inverse of sin is written sin−1 or arcsin. The inverse of cos is cos−1 or arccos. The inverse of tan is tan−1 or arctan. The two spellings mean the same.Each one is the reflection of its original graph in the line y=x, but only for part of the graph (the restricted domain).

    Watch out: sin−1x does not mean 1sinx. That is cosecx. Sine, cosine and tangent repeat, so they have no inverse over the whole graph. Restrict the domain to a part where each value appears once. This gives one answer, the Principal value.

    Flip it: The original function takes an angle and gives a ratio; the inverse takes the ratio and gives the angle.

    See also: Inverse sine (arcsin, sin−¹), Inverse cosine (arccos, cos−¹), Inverse tangent (arctan, tan−¹), Principal value

    inversely proportional Algebra and functions Year 1

    Two quantities are linked so that the first equals a fixed number divided by the second.

    Examples:y∝1x means y=kx. The graph of y against x is a reciprocal graph.The graph of y against 1x is a straight line through the origin.

    Watch out: The product xy stays constant. Doubling x halves y.

    See also: proportional (∝), reciprocal graph

    irrational number Proof Year 1

    A number that cannot be written as one integer divided by another. Its decimal never ends and never repeats.

    Examples:2, π and 5 are irrational.A rational number plus an irrational number is irrational: 3+2 is irrational.

    Watch out: The square roots of square numbers are rational: 9=3. And 227 is a rational number close to π, not π itself.

    Flip it: Every real number (ℝ) is either rational or irrational, never both.

    See also: rational number, proof by contradiction, integer

    Iteration Numerical methods Year 2

    Repeating the same calculation again and again, each time using the answer as the next input, to get closer and closer to a solution.

    Examples:Start with x0=1.3 and repeat xn+1=xn+13. The values are x1=1.3200, x2=1.3238, x3=1.3245, getting closer to 1.3247.A calculator can do this: type the starting value, press equals, then apply the formula to the answer each time (using the ANS key).

    Watch out: Keep full calculator accuracy while iterating and round only at the end. Write the values in a list: x1, x2, x3 and so on.

    See also: Iterative formula, Starting value, Convergence, Newton-Raphson method

    Iterative formula Numerical methods Year 2

    A rule of the form x(n+1) = g(x(n)), read as "x n plus 1 equals g of x n". It gives each new approximation from the one before it.

    Examples:To solve x3−x−1=0, rearrange it as x3=x+1, so x=x+13. This gives the iterative formula xn+1=xn+13.The same equation can also be rearranged as x=x3−1, giving xn+1=xn3−1. From x0=1.3 this formula moves away from the root. Different rearrangements behave differently.

    Watch out: The rearrangement must still be equivalent to the original equation: a fixed point of the formula must be a root. Whether it works depends on the rearrangement, so test it.

    See also: Iteration, Fixed point, Convergence, Divergence

    L

    laws of indices Algebra and functions Year 1

    The rules for powers of the same base: add the indices to multiply, subtract them to divide, and multiply them to raise a power to a power.

    Examples:am×an=am+naman=am−n(am)n=am×na0=1 (for a≠0).

    Watch out: The first two laws need the same base: 23×32 cannot be combined by adding indices. Also (a+b)2 is not a2+b2.

    Flip it: Read the laws backwards to split one power into smaller pieces: xa+b=xa×xb.

    See also: index (power), negative index, fractional index

    limit Differentiation Year 1

    The value that an expression gets closer and closer to as another quantity gets closer and closer to a given value.

    Examples:As h gets closer to 0, (2+h)2−4h gets closer to 4.Expand the top: 4h+h2h=4+h. When h is very small, 4+h is almost 4. We write limh→0(2+h)2−4h=4. Read it as "the limit, as h tends to 0, of this fraction is 4". Here "tends to 0" means "gets close to 0".

    Watch out: Do not put h=0 into the fraction. That gives 0 over 0, which has no value. Simplify first, then let h get close to 0. A limit describes where an expression is going. The expression does not have to reach it.

    See also: differentiation from first principles, derivative

    Limit of a sequence Sequences and series Year 2

    The value that the terms of a sequence get closer to, as close as you like, as n gets bigger.

    Examples:un=3+4n gives 7, 5, 4.33 … The terms get closer to 3, so the limit is 3.un+1=un2+3: if there is a limit L, then L=L2+3, so L=6.

    Watch out: The terms need not ever reach the limit. Only use "replace un and un+1 with L" when the sequence does converge. For this rule it does, because each step halves the distance to 6.

    See also: Convergent, Recurrence relation

    limits of integration Integration Year 1

    The two numbers on an integral sign. The lower limit is the value of the variable where the integration starts. The upper limit is where the integration stops.

    Example: In ∫132xdx, the lower limit is 1 and the upper limit is 3. They are values of x.

    Watch out: The limits belong to the variable in the dx. If you substitute a new variable, change the limits too. See changing the limits.

    See also: definite integral, changing the limits

    Line meeting a circle Coordinate geometry Year 1

    A straight line meets a circle at two points, at one point (when it is a tangent) or at no point.

    Examples:Method: substitute the line’s equation into the circle’s equation. You get a quadratic in one letter.Circle x2+y2=25. The line y=3 gives x2=16, so x=4 or x=−4: two points.The line y=5 gives x2=0, so x=0: one point, so it is a tangent.The line y=7 gives x2=−24: no solutions, so the line misses the circle.

    Watch out: Find both coordinates of each point. After you find x, substitute it into the line’s equation to get y.

    Flip it: The discriminant of the quadratic tells you how many points: positive means two, zero means one (a tangent) and negative means none.

    See also: Tangent, Chord, Point of contact

    Line segment Coordinate geometry Year 1

    The part of a straight line between two end points. It has a length. A whole line goes on for ever.

    Example: The line segment AB joins A (1, 1) to B (5, 4). Its Midpoint is (3, 2.5) and its length is 5.

    Watch out: A line segment stops at A and B. An equation such as y=2x describes the whole line, so give the x-values when you mean a segment.

    See also: Midpoint, Distance between two points

    Linear model Coordinate geometry Year 1

    A straight-line equation used to describe a real situation, where one quantity changes at a constant rate with another.

    Examples:A taxi charges 3 pounds to start and 2 pounds per kilometre. The fare is F=3+2d.The gradient 2 is the rate (pounds per kilometre). The intercept 3 is the fixed charge.

    Watch out: A model only works in a sensible range. A distance of −4 km makes no sense. Say which assumption you made: here, that the rate never changes.

    See also: Equation of a straight line, y = mx + c, Gradient, y-intercept

    Log-log graph Exponentials and logs Year 1

    A graph with log y on the vertical axis and log x on the horizontal axis. It is a straight line when y = a x^n, with gradient n and vertical intercept log a.

    Examples:y=3x2 gives logy=2logx+log3. The gradient is 2 and the intercept is log3=0.477.If a graph of logy against logx passes through (0, 0.477) and has gradient 2, then loga=0.477, so a=3, and n=2.

    Watch out: The intercept is loga, not a. To find a, work backwards: a=10loga for logarithms to base 10, or a=elna for natural logarithms.

    Flip it: It turns a power law into a straight line, while a Semi-log graph does the same for exponential growth.

    See also: Reducing to a straight line (linearising), Semi-log graph, Power law of logarithms

    Logarithm (log) Exponentials and logs Year 1

    The power you must raise a base a to, to get a given number x. For example, you raise 2 to the power 3 to get 8.

    Examples:log28=3 because 23=8. Read log28 as "log to the base 2 of 8". log101000=3 because 103=1000.logax=y means exactly the same as ay=x. Two ways of writing one fact.Some values are always the same: loga1=0 and logaa=1.

    Watch out: You can only take the logarithm of a positive number: logax needs x>0. The base must be positive and not 1. A logarithm is a power, so it can be negative or a fraction: log2(14)=−2.

    Flip it: It undoes an Exponential function: loga(ax)=x and alogax=x. See Logarithm and exponential are inverses.

    See also: Base, Common logarithm (log base 10), Natural logarithm (ln), Logarithm and exponential are inverses, Graph of a logarithm

    Logarithm and exponential are inverses Exponentials and logs Year 1

    Taking a logarithm to base a and raising a to a power undo each other, in either order.

    Examples:loga(ax)=x and alogax=x.ln(ex)=x and elnx=x. For example eln5=5 and log10(107)=7.

    Watch out: It only works when the base of the logarithm and the base of the power are the same. 10ln5 is not 5.

    Flip it: This is why the graph of a logarithm is the reflection of the matching exponential graph in the line y=x.

    See also: Logarithm (log), Natural logarithm (ln), Graph of a logarithm, Exponential equation

    lowest terms Proof Year 2

    A fraction is in lowest terms when its top and bottom have no common factor except 1.

    Examples:68 is not in lowest terms, because both numbers divide by 2. In lowest terms it is 34.In a proof, "a over b in lowest terms" means a and b are not both even.

    Watch out: In the proof that 2 is irrational, the argument ends with a and b both even. That contradicts lowest terms.

    See also: rational number, proof by contradiction

    M

    Magnitude Vectors Year 1

    The size, or length, of a vector. You find it by using Pythagoras’ theorem on the components. It is never negative.

    Examples:For a = (34): |a|=32+42=5.Read |a| as "the magnitude of a".

    Watch out: The signs disappear when you square. A magnitude is never negative. In general |a+b| is not |a|+|b|. The two sides are equal only when a and b point the same way.

    See also: Component, Unit vector, Distance in three dimensions

    many-to-one function Algebra and functions Year 2

    A function where at least two different inputs give the same output.

    Examples:f(x)=x2: f(2)=4 and f(−2)=4.On the graph, a horizontal line meets the curve more than once.

    Watch out: A many-to-one rule is still a function. A one-to-many rule is not.

    Flip it: Restrict the domain, for example x≥0, to make it one-to-one. Then it has an inverse.

    See also: one-to-one function, inverse function, domain

    mapping Algebra and functions Year 2

    A rule that takes each member of one set to a member of another set. A function is a mapping where each input has only one output.

    Examples:x↦x2 maps 2 to 4 and −2 to 4.A mapping where one input gives two outputs, such as x↦±x, is not a function.

    Watch out: Every function is a mapping. Not every mapping is a function.

    See also: function, one-to-one function, many-to-one function

    maximum point Differentiation Year 1

    A point where the curve is higher than at every point close to it. The gradient is zero there. It is positive a little to the left of the point and negative a little to the right.

    Example: The curve y=−x2+4x has dydx=−2x+4. This is zero at x=2. The second derivative is −2, which is negative, so (2, 4) is a maximum point.

    Watch out: This is a local maximum: nearby points are lower, but a different part of the curve may be higher. The maximum value is the y-coordinate, not the x-coordinate.

    Flip it: A minimum point is the same idea upside down.

    See also: minimum point, stationary point, nature of a stationary point, global maximum and minimum

    Midpoint Coordinate geometry Year 1

    The point exactly halfway between two points on a line segment. Its coordinates are the averages of the end points’ coordinates.

    Examples:The midpoint of (1, 1) and (5, 4) is (1+52,1+42)=(3,2.5).The general formula is (x1+x22,y1+y22).

    Watch out: Add the coordinates, then halve. Do not subtract: subtracting gives the change, not the middle.

    Flip it: Given the midpoint M and one end A, the other end is 2M−A, coordinate by coordinate. If M is (3, 2.5) and A is (1, 1), the other end is (2×3−1,2×2.5−1)=(5,4).

    See also: Line segment, Perpendicular bisector, Diameter

    minimum point Differentiation Year 1

    A point where the curve is lower than at every point close to it. The gradient is zero there. It is negative a little to the left of the point and positive a little to the right.

    Example: The curve y=x2−4x has dydx=2x−4. This is zero at x=2. The second derivative is 2, which is positive, so (2, -4) is a minimum point.

    Watch out: This is a local minimum. Another part of the curve may go lower. The minimum value is the y-coordinate, not the x-coordinate.

    Flip it: A maximum point is the same idea upside down.

    See also: maximum point, stationary point, nature of a stationary point, global maximum and minimum

    modulus Algebra and functions Year 2

    The size of a number, ignoring its sign. It is the distance of the number from zero on a number line. It is written with vertical bars.

    Examples:|5|=5 and |−5|=5.Read |x| as "the modulus of x".|x−2| is the distance from x to 2. So |x−2|=3 gives x=5 or x=−1.|x−2|<3 gives −1<x<5.

    Watch out: A modulus is never negative. |x|=3 gives two answers, x=3 or x=−3. Also |a+b| is not usually |a|+|b|.

    See also: modulus function, inequality, function

    modulus function Algebra and functions Year 2

    A function written with vertical bars around an expression, such as y equals the modulus of f of x. The graph of that function never goes below the x-axis.

    Examples:y=|f(x)|: keep the parts of y=f(x) above the x-axis, and reflect the parts below it in the x-axis.y=f(|x|): keep the part with x≥0, and draw its reflection in the y-axis. Delete the part of the original graph where x is negative.

    Watch out: The two graphs are different. y=|f(x)| reflects the parts of the graph of f that are below the x-axis upwards. y=f(|x|) keeps the right-hand part of the graph of f and reflects it in the y-axis, so its graph is symmetric about the y-axis. To solve a modulus equation, check each answer in the original equation.

    See also: modulus, reflection (of a graph), function

    N

    Natural exponential function (e^x) Exponentials and logs Year 1

    The function y = e to the power x, which is the exponential function whose gradient at every point equals its height.

    Examples:e0=1, e1=2.718, e−1=0.368. The graph goes through (0, 1), is always above the x-axis and has the x-axis as an asymptote.It can also be written expx. On a calculator, use the ex key.

    Watch out: Do not write e2x as (ex)×2. The brackets matter: e2x=(ex)2. Also ex+y=ex×ey, but ex+y is not ex+ey.

    Flip it: Its inverse is the Natural logarithm (ln), lnx: elnx=x and ln(ex)=x.

    See also: The number e, Natural logarithm (ln), Exponential function

    Natural logarithm (ln) Exponentials and logs Year 1

    The logarithm to base e, written ln x. It is the inverse of the function e to the power x.

    Examples:lnx=y means ey=x. So lne=1, ln1=0 and ln(e3)=3.Solve ex=5: x=ln5=1.61 to 3 significant figures.

    Watch out: ln and log are different keys on the calculator: ln is base e, log is base 10. lnx is only defined for x>0. ln(x+y) is not lnx+lny.

    Flip it: Its graph is the graph of y=ex reflected in the line y=x. It has the y-axis as an asymptote and passes through (1, 0).

    See also: Logarithm (log), The number e, Natural exponential function (e^x), Graph of a logarithm

    nature of a stationary point Differentiation Year 1

    Whether a stationary point is a maximum or a minimum. (In Year 2 you also meet a stationary point that is neither: a point of inflection.)

    Examples:For y=x3−3x: d2ydx2=6x.At x=1 it is 6, which is positive: a minimum. At x=−1 it is −6, which is negative: a maximum.Second-derivative test: positive means a minimum, negative means a maximum. Gradient test: check the sign of dydx a little to the left and a little to the right of the point.

    Watch out: If the second derivative is 0, the test tells you nothing. y=x4 has a minimum at (0, 0), and d2ydx2=0 there. Use the gradient test instead. In Year 2 you meet points of inflection: do not say a point is one without checking.

    See also: stationary point, second derivative, maximum point, minimum point, point of inflection

    nCr (binomial coefficient) Sequences and series Year 1

    The number of ways to choose r things from n, written nCr and read "n choose r". It equals n! divided by the product of r! and (n - r)!.

    Examples:The formula is nCr = n!r!(n−r)!.For example, C25 = 5!2!3!=12012=10.Your calculator has an nCr button.

    Watch out: nCr is the same as nC(n - r), so C25 = C35. Also C0n = Cnn = 1. You need r to be no bigger than n.

    Flip it: The values of nCr are the numbers in row n of Pascal’s triangle.

    See also: Factorial, n!, Pascal’s triangle, Binomial expansion

    negation Proof Year 2

    The statement that says the opposite. It is true exactly when the original statement is false.

    Examples:Statement: "n is even". Negation: "n is not even", which for an integer means "n is odd".Statement: "every prime is odd". Negation: "at least one prime is not odd".

    Watch out: The negation of "all" is "at least one is not". It is not "none". The negation of x>3 is x≤3, not x<3.

    See also: proof by contradiction, statement, counterexample

    negative index Algebra and functions Year 1

    An index below zero. It means "one over": a to the power minus n is one divided by a to the power n.

    Examples:2−3=123=18(23)−2=(32)2=94

    Watch out: A negative index does not make the number negative. 2−3 is 18, not −8.

    Flip it: A reciprocal turns a positive index into a negative one: 1x4=x−4.

    See also: index (power), laws of indices, fractional index

    Negative of a vector Vectors Year 1

    A vector with the same magnitude as a but the opposite direction, written −a.

    Examples:If a is (2−3), then −a is (−23).BA→=−AB→.

    Watch out: Change the sign of every component. a+(−a) is the Zero vector.

    See also: Vector subtraction, Zero vector, Vector notation

    Negative reciprocal Coordinate geometry Year 1

    What you get when you turn a number upside down and change its sign. For lines that are not horizontal or vertical, the gradients of perpendicular lines are negative reciprocals.

    Examples:The negative reciprocal of 3 is −13.The negative reciprocal of −25 is 52.Check: a number times its negative reciprocal is −1.

    Watch out: Do both steps. Turning upside down only gives the reciprocal. Changing the sign only gives the negative.

    See also: Perpendicular, Gradient

    Newton-Raphson method Numerical methods Year 2

    An iterative method that finds a root of f(x) = 0 by following the tangent to the curve at each approximation until it meets the x-axis.

    Examples:The formula is xn+1 = xn − f(xn) / f′(xn), where f′ is the derivative of f.Find 2 using f(x)=x2−2, so f′(x) = 2x. From x0=2: x1=2−24=1.5 and x2=1.5−0.253=1.41667. The value of 2 is 1.41421 to 5 decimal places.

    Watch out: It fails if f′(xn) = 0, because the tangent is flat and never reaches the x-axis. A starting value near a stationary point can send it far away, or to a different root. It is much faster than most other iterations when it works.

    Flip it: It is an Iterative formula built from the gradient of the curve, so it needs the derivative of f.

    See also: Iteration, Iterative formula, Starting value, Convergence

    Normal Coordinate geometry Year 1

    The straight line through a point on a curve or circle that is at a right angle to the tangent there.

    Examples:The normal to x2+y2=25 at (3, 4) is perpendicular to the tangent, so its gradient is 43.y−4=43(x−3) simplifies to 3y=4x. It passes through the origin, which is the centre.

    Watch out: Find the gradient of the tangent first, then take the Negative reciprocal. In everyday speech normal means usual. In maths it means at right angles.

    Flip it: The normal to a circle always passes through its centre.

    See also: Tangent, Perpendicular, Negative reciprocal

    normal to a curve Differentiation Year 1

    The straight line through a point on a curve that is at right angles to the tangent at that point.

    Example: On y=x2 at (3, 9), the tangent has gradient 6. The normal has gradient −1/6. Its equation is y−9=−1/6(x−3).

    Watch out: First find the gradient of the tangent. Then take the negative reciprocal: write 1 divided by that gradient, and change its sign. If the tangent is horizontal, the normal is vertical, with equation x=a. Do not use the derivative itself as the gradient of the normal.

    Flip it: Normal and tangent are a pair. The two gradients multiply to give −1.

    See also: tangent to a curve, gradient of a curve

    nth term (position-to-term rule) Sequences and series Year 2

    A formula that gives any term of a sequence directly from its position n.

    Examples:un=2n+1 gives u1=3, u2=5, u3=7 …The 10th term is u10=2×10+1=21.

    Watch out: Substitute the position n, not the value of the term. To check a formula, test it on the first two terms.

    Flip it: A term-to-term rule gets one term from the one before. The nth term formula gives any term directly.

    See also: Term-to-term rule, Arithmetic sequence, Geometric sequence

    Numerical integration Numerical methods Year 2

    Finding an approximate value of a definite integral with a step-by-step method, when the function cannot be integrated exactly.

    Examples:∫01e−x2dx has no answer in terms of the functions you know. The Trapezium rule gives an estimate.You can also use it to check an answer found by integrating, like checking 2.75 against 83.

    Watch out: The answer is an approximation, so say "to 3 decimal places" or similar. More strips give a better approximation.

    See also: Trapezium rule, Numerical method

    Numerical method Numerical methods Year 2

    A step-by-step method that finds an approximate answer to a problem which cannot be solved exactly by algebra.

    Examples:x3−x−1=0 cannot be solved by factorising or by a formula you know. A numerical method finds x=1.3247 to 4 decimal places, or as many as you need.Three methods in this book: the Change of sign method, Iteration (including Newton-Raphson method) and the Trapezium rule.

    Watch out: A numerical answer is an approximation. State how accurate the answer is (for example "to 3 decimal places"), and show the working that proves this.

    See also: Change of sign, Iteration, Newton-Raphson method, Trapezium rule

    O

    odd number Proof Year 1

    An integer that is one more than a multiple of 2. Written with a letter, an odd number is 2n + 1, where n is an integer.

    Examples:The odd numbers: −3, −1, 1, 3, 5, 7.In a proof, call an odd number 2n+1. The product of two odd numbers is (2a+1)(2b+1)=2(2ab+a+b)+1, which is odd.

    Watch out: You can also write an odd number as 2n−1. Use a different letter for each odd number in the same proof.

    Flip it: An integer that is not odd is even number.

    See also: even number, integer, consecutive integers, proof by deduction

    one-to-one function Algebra and functions Year 2

    A function where each output comes from exactly one input.

    Examples:f(x)=2x+1 is one-to-one.On a graph, no horizontal line meets the curve more than once.

    Watch out: Only a one-to-one function has an inverse function.

    Flip it: A function where two inputs share an output is many-to-one function.

    See also: many-to-one function, inverse function, function

    optimisation Differentiation Year 1

    Finding the largest or smallest possible value of a quantity, usually by differentiating and setting the derivative to zero.

    Examples:A rectangle has a perimeter of 40 cm. Its width is x cm, so its length is 20−x cm.Area: A=x(20−x)=20x−x2. Then dAdx=20−2x=0 gives x=10.d2Adx2=−2 is negative, so this is a maximum. The largest area is 100 cm².

    Watch out: Write the quantity using one variable first. Then differentiate. Check whether the point is a maximum or a minimum, whichever the question asks for. Give the value the question asks for, with units. Check that your answer is possible in the situation, such as a length that is positive.

    See also: maximum point, minimum point, global maximum and minimum, rate of change

    Ordinate (y-value) Numerical methods Year 2

    The height of the curve at one of the equally spaced x-values used in the trapezium rule.

    Examples:For y=x2 from 0 to 2 with 4 strips, the x-values are 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2. The ordinates are y0=0, y1=0.25, y2=1, y3=2.25, y4=4.Each ordinate is a vertical side of one or two trapezia.

    Watch out: Number them from 0: y0 is the first. Put your calculator in radian mode if the function has sin or cos and no degree sign.

    See also: Trapezium rule, Strip width

    Oscillating sequence Sequences and series Year 2

    A sequence whose terms keep going up and then down (or the reverse) instead of moving in one direction.

    Example: un=(−1)n gives −1, 1, −1, 1 … un=(−12)n gives −12,14,−18 …

    Watch out: An oscillating sequence may still settle on a limit. The second example gets closer and closer to 0. The first example does not settle.

    See also: Periodic sequence, Convergent, Divergent

    Over- and underestimate Numerical methods Year 2

    The trapezium rule gives an answer that is too big if the curve bends upwards. It gives an answer that is too small if the curve bends downwards. The straight tops of the trapezia lie above the curve in the first case and below it in the second.

    Examples:For y=x2, the curve bends upwards (the second derivative is positive). Each straight top lies above the curve, so the trapezium rule gives too big an answer: 2.75 instead of 2.667.For y=x, the curve bends downwards. The straight tops lie below the curve, so the rule gives too small an answer.

    Watch out: Justify your answer by looking at the shape of the curve over the whole interval, with a sketch. If the curve bends one way in part of the interval and the other way in the rest, you cannot say. Using more strips makes the estimate better.

    Flip it: A curve that bends upwards has f″(x) > 0 (second derivative positive): the trapezium rule overestimates. A curve that bends downwards has f″(x) < 0: it underestimates.

    See also: Trapezium rule, Numerical integration

    P

    parabola Algebra and functions Year 1

    The U-shaped curve that is the graph of a quadratic. It opens upwards if the coefficient of x squared is positive, and downwards if it is negative.

    Examples:y=x2−4x+3 is a parabola that opens upwards. Its lowest point is (2,−1).y=−x2 opens downwards.

    Watch out: Both arms go on for ever. A parabola does not level off or curve back, as a circle does.

    See also: vertex (of a parabola), axis of symmetry, quadratic, root (of an equation or function)

    Parallel lines Coordinate geometry Year 1

    Lines in a flat plane that never meet. They have the same gradient.

    Example: y=2x+1 and y=2x−2 are parallel. Both have gradient 2.

    Watch out: Two lines with the same gradient and the same y-intercept are the same line, not two parallel lines. Check the equations are in the form y=mx+c before you compare gradients.

    Flip it: If two lines have different gradients, they must meet at exactly one point.

    See also: Gradient, Perpendicular

    Parallel vectors Vectors Year 1

    Vectors that point in the same direction or in opposite directions. One is a scalar multiple of the other.

    Examples:(23) and (69) are parallel, because the second is 3 times the first.(−4−6) is −2 times (23), so it is parallel too, pointing the opposite way.

    Watch out: Parallel vectors need not be equal and need not be the same length. Check that the components are in the same ratio. 2i+3j and 4i+5j are not parallel.

    Flip it: If a=kb for some number k, the vectors are parallel.

    See also: Scalar multiple, Collinear

    Parameter Coordinate geometry Year 2

    A third variable, often t or the angle theta, that both x and y depend on. As the parameter changes, the point (x, y) moves along a curve.

    Example: Take x=2t and y=t2. When t=3, the point is (6, 9). When t=−1, it is (-2, 1).

    Watch out: The parameter is not a coordinate. It often stands for time, but it need not. Give its range, such as 0≤t≤3, when the question does.

    Flip it: Remove the parameter to get an equation in x and y alone. That is the Cartesian equation.

    See also: Parametric equations, Eliminate the parameter, Cartesian equation

    parametric differentiation Differentiation Year 2

    Finding dy by dx for a curve where x and y both depend on a third letter, called the parameter. Divide the derivative of y by the derivative of x.

    Example: For x=t2 and y=2t: dxdt=2t and dydt=2. So dydx=dydt/dxdt=22t=1t.

    Watch out: Put dy by dt on the top and dx by dt on the bottom, not the other way round. If dxdt=0 the formula fails. There the tangent is vertical, as long as dydt is not also 0. The answer contains t, so find the value of t at the given point first.

    Flip it: This is the chain rule: dydx=dydt×dtdx.

    See also: chain rule, implicit differentiation, tangent to a curve

    Parametric equations Coordinate geometry Year 2

    A pair of equations that give x and y separately, each using a third variable, the parameter.

    Examples:x=3cost, y=3sint for 0≤t<2π is the circle x2+y2=9, with centre the origin and radius 3.x=2t, y=t2 is the parabola y=x24.

    Watch out: The values allowed for t decide how much of the curve you get. x=2t,y=t2 for 0≤t≤3 is only the part of the parabola from (0, 0) to (6, 9).

    Flip it: Each value of t gives one point (x, y). To go the other way, eliminate t.

    See also: Parameter, Cartesian equation, Eliminate the parameter

    partial fractions Algebra and functions Year 2

    Writing one algebraic fraction as a sum of simpler fractions. Each simpler fraction has one factor of the original bottom as its own bottom.

    Examples:3x+5(x+1)(x+2)=Ax+1+Bx+2.Multiply both sides by (x+1)(x+2): 3x+5=A(x+2)+B(x+1). Substitute x=−1: 2=A. Substitute x=−2: −1=−B, so B=1.So the fraction is 2x+1+1x+2.

    Watch out: A repeated factor needs a fraction for each power. For (x−2)2, write Bx−2+C(x−2)2.

    Flip it: Adding the simple fractions over a common denominator gives back the original fraction.

    See also: algebraic fraction, improper algebraic fraction

    particular solution Integration Year 2

    The one solution of a differential equation that fits given extra information, found by using it to work out the constant.

    Example: The general solution of dydx=2y is y=Ae2x. Given y=3 when x=0: 3=A. The particular solution is y=3e2x.

    Watch out: Find the general solution first, then put in the condition. Do not use the condition before you integrate.

    See also: general solution, initial condition, family of solution curves

    Pascal’s triangle Sequences and series Year 1

    A triangle of numbers in which each number is the sum of the two above it. Row n gives the binomial coefficients for a power n.

    Examples:Rows 0 to 5: 1 / 1 1 / 1 2 1 / 1 3 3 1 / 1 4 6 4 1 / 1 5 10 10 5 1.Row 4 gives (a+b)4=a4+4a3b+6a2b2+4ab3+b4.

    Watch out: The top row, a single 1, is row 0. Row n goes with the power n. Pascal’s triangle is quick for small n. For large n use nCr.

    See also: nCr (binomial coefficient), Binomial expansion

    Period Trigonometry Year 1

    The length of one full cycle of a repeating graph. It is how far you move along the x-axis before the graph repeats.

    Examples:y=sinx has period 360°. y=tanx has period 180°.y=sin(3x) has period 360°3=120°. In general, y=sin(bx) has period 360°b.

    Watch out: A bigger number inside the bracket gives a shorter period, because the graph is squashed. Divide 360° by that number. Do not multiply.

    Flip it: A function that repeats like this is called periodic. The Amplitude says how tall the repeat is; the period says how wide.

    See also: Amplitude, Sine (sin), Tangent (tan), the trigonometric function

    Periodic sequence Sequences and series Year 2

    A sequence that repeats the same block of terms again and again. The number of terms in one block is the period (or order).

    Examples:1, 3, 2, 1, 3, 2, 1, 3, 2 … has period 3. In symbols, un+3=un.To find u100: 100=3×33+1, so the 100th term matches the 1st term, which is 1.un=sin(90n°) gives 1, 0, −1, 0, 1, 0 … with period 4.

    Watch out: Divide the position by the period and look at the remainder. A remainder of 0 means the last term of the block, not the first.

    See also: Recurrence relation, Oscillating sequence

    Perpendicular Coordinate geometry Year 1

    Meeting at a right angle (90 degrees).

    Example: The lines y=2x and y=−12x+2.5 are perpendicular. The gradients are 2 and −12, and 2×(−12)=−1.

    Watch out: In everyday speech perpendicular often means upright. In maths it means at a right angle to something else, in any direction. The rule that the gradients multiply to give -1 does not cover horizontal and vertical lines. A horizontal line is perpendicular to a vertical line, and a vertical line has no gradient.

    Flip it: Two lines that are neither horizontal nor vertical are perpendicular exactly when their gradients are negative reciprocals.

    See also: Negative reciprocal, Parallel lines, Perpendicular bisector, Normal

    Perpendicular bisector Coordinate geometry Year 1

    The line that cuts a line segment in half and meets it at a right angle.

    Examples:Find the perpendicular bisector of A (1, 1) and B (5, 3).Midpoint: (3, 2). Gradient of AB: 24=12. Perpendicular gradient: −2.Line through (3, 2) with gradient −2: y−2=−2(x−3), so y=−2x+8.

    Watch out: You need both facts: it passes through the Midpoint, and its gradient is the Negative reciprocal of the gradient of AB. Using only one gives the wrong line.

    Flip it: Every point on the perpendicular bisector is the same distance from A as from B.

    See also: Midpoint, Perpendicular, Perpendicular from the centre to a chord

    Perpendicular from the centre to a chord Coordinate geometry Year 1

    A line from the centre of a circle that meets a chord at a right angle cuts the chord in half.

    Examples:A circle passes through (0, 0) and (6, 0). The perpendicular bisector of that chord is x=3.The centre is on that line, so its x-coordinate is 3.

    Watch out: It works for a chord, not for any line. The line must come from the centre and meet the chord at 90 degrees.

    Flip it: The perpendicular bisector of any chord passes through the centre. Two such bisectors meet at the centre, which is how you find the circle through three points.

    See also: Chord, Perpendicular bisector, Centre of a circle

    Point dividing a line in a ratio Vectors Year 1

    A point P on the line AB with AP : PB = m : n. To find its position vector, start at A and move the fraction m/(m + n) of the way to B.

    Examples:If AP:PB=m:n, then p=a+mm+n(b−a)=na+mbm+n.A (1, 2), B (7, 8), AP:PB=1:2: p=2a+b3=13 (912) = (34).

    Watch out: The part of the ratio for A goes with b, and the part for B goes with a. Check: when P is nearer A, it should be nearer a in the formula.

    See also: Position vector, Collinear, Vector proof

    Point of contact Coordinate geometry Year 1

    The one point where a tangent touches a circle or curve.

    Example: The tangent 3x+4y=25 touches x2+y2=25 at (3, 4). That point is the point of contact.

    Watch out: To find it, solve the line and the circle together. The equation you get has a repeated solution, so its discriminant is 0.

    See also: Tangent, Line meeting a circle

    point of inflection Differentiation Year 2

    A point where a curve changes from concave to convex, or from convex to concave. The second derivative changes sign there.

    Examples:y=x3−3x2 has d2ydx2=6x−6.This is zero at x=1. The second derivative is negative to the left of x=1 and positive to the right, so (1, -2) is a point of inflection. The gradient there is −3, so it is not a stationary point.

    Watch out: Having d2ydx2=0 is not enough. y=x4 has d2ydx2=0 at 0, but the second derivative does not change sign, so there is no inflection. Check the sign on both sides. A point of inflection can be stationary or not.

    See also: concave, convex, second derivative, stationary point

    Point-gradient form, y - y1 = m(x - x1) Coordinate geometry Year 1

    The equation of the line with gradient m through the point (x1, y1), written y - y1 = m(x - x1).

    Examples:Gradient 2 through (2, 1): y−1=2(x−2). Expand to get y=2x−3.Through (1, 1) and (3, 5): the gradient is 2 (see Gradient). Use either point: y−1=2(x−1) or y−5=2(x−3). Both give y=2x−1.

    Watch out: Subtract the point from x and y. Through (2, -3), the left side is y−(−3), which is y+3.

    Flip it: Rearranging into y=mx+c tells you the y-intercept.

    See also: Equation of a straight line, y = mx + c, Gradient

    polynomial Algebra and functions Year 1

    An expression made by adding terms. Each term is a number times a power of x. Each power is a whole number: 0, 1, 2, 3 and so on.

    Examples:3x4−2x2+x−7 is a polynomial.x+1 and 1x+x are not polynomials, because each has a power that is not a whole number of 0 or more.

    Watch out: A number on its own, such as 7, is a polynomial. A polynomial can have a missing power: x3+1 has no x2 term.

    See also: degree (of a polynomial), coefficient, constant term, cubic, quartic, factor theorem

    polynomial division Algebra and functions Year 1

    Dividing one polynomial by another, in the way you do long division with numbers, to get a quotient and a remainder.

    Examples:x3+2x2−5x−6=(x−2)(x2+4x+3), so dividing by (x−2) gives quotient x2+4x+3 and remainder 0.Dividing the same polynomial by (x−1) gives quotient x2+3x−2 and remainder −8.

    Watch out: Write a zero for any missing power, such as 0x2, so the columns line up. At each step, divide the highest power of what is left by the highest power of the divisor (the polynomial you divide by).

    See also: quotient, remainder, remainder theorem, factor theorem

    Position vector Vectors Year 1

    The vector from the origin O to a point. Its components are the coordinates of the point.

    Examples:The point A (3, -2) has position vector OA→=a, which is (3−2).For any two points, AB→=b−a: the end minus the start.The midpoint of AB has position vector a+b2.

    Watch out: A position vector always starts at the origin. The vector AB→ between two points does not.

    See also: Displacement, Column vector, Point dividing a line in a ratio

    Power law of logarithms Exponentials and logs Year 1

    The rule that the logarithm of a number raised to a power is the power multiplied by the logarithm of the number.

    Examples:loga(xk)=klogaxlog10(53)=3log105. And logax=12logax.It is how you solve 3x=20: take logarithms of both sides to get xlog103=log1020, so x=log1020log103=2.73.

    Watch out: The power k must apply to the number inside the logarithm. In (logax)2, the square applies to the whole logarithm, so the rule cannot be used.

    See also: Product law of logarithms, Quotient law of logarithms, Exponential equation

    prime number Proof Year 1

    An integer greater than 1 with exactly two factors: 1 and itself.

    Examples:The first primes: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13.9 is not prime, because 3×3=9.

    Watch out: 1 is not prime, because it has only one factor. 2 is prime, and it is the only even prime.

    See also: proof by contradiction, integer

    Principal value Trigonometry Year 1

    The single angle that a calculator gives when you press an inverse key such as sin−¹. It always lies in a fixed range that depends on the key.

    Examples:sin−¹(0.5) gives 30°, and sin−¹(−0.5) gives −30°. The principal values of sin−¹ lie between −90° and 90°.Solve sinx=0.5 for 0°≤x≤360°. The calculator gives 30°. The other solution is 150°, found by symmetry.

    Watch out: The calculator gives one answer, but a trigonometric equation can have several. The calculator value is where you start, not the whole solution. Principal values: sin−1 gives −90° to 90°. cos−1 gives 0° to 180°. tan−1 gives −90° to 90°, not including −90° or 90°.

    See also: Trigonometric equation, CAST diagram, Inverse trigonometric functions (sin−¹, arcsin)

    Product law of logarithms Exponentials and logs Year 1

    The rule that adding two logarithms with the same base gives the logarithm of the product.

    Examples:logax+logay=loga(xy)log104+log1025=log10100=2.

    Watch out: Both logarithms must have the same base. The rule does not apply to loga(x+y). It is not equal to logax+logay.

    Flip it: Read from right to left, it splits a product into a sum: loga(6x)=loga6+logax.

    See also: Quotient law of logarithms, Power law of logarithms, Logarithm (log)

    product rule Differentiation Year 2

    The rule for differentiating two functions multiplied together: the first times the derivative of the second, plus the second times the derivative of the first.

    Examples:If y=u×v, then dydx=u×dvdx+v×dudx.For y=x2sin(x), let u=x2 and v=sin(x). Then dydx=x2cos(x)+2xsin(x).

    Watch out: The derivative of a product is not the product of the derivatives. Use the rule only when both factors involve x. 5x2 is a constant times a function, so you do not need it.

    Flip it: Integration by parts is the product rule run backwards.

    See also: quotient rule, chain rule, implicit differentiation

    proof Proof Year 1

    A chain of logical steps, each following from the one before, that shows a statement is true in every possible case.

    Examples:To prove that the sum of two even numbers is even, write them as 2a and 2b.Then 2a+2b=2(a+b), which is 2 times an integer, so it is even.

    Watch out: Checking examples is not a proof. A thousand examples that work do not cover the thousand-and-first.

    Flip it: To show a statement is false you need only one counterexample.

    See also: proof by deduction, proof by exhaustion, proof by contradiction, counterexample, show that

    proof by contradiction Proof Year 2

    A proof that assumes the statement is false, then shows this leads to something impossible, so the statement must be true.

    Examples:Prove that 2 is irrational.Assume 2=ab with the fraction in lowest terms. Then a2=2b2, so a2 is even, so a is even.Write a=2k. Then 4k2=2b2, so b2=2k2, so b is even.Now a and b are both even, which contradicts "lowest terms". So the assumption was wrong.

    Watch out: Write the opposite of the statement with care. The opposite of "all" is "at least one is not", never "none". See negation.

    Flip it: A counterexample disproves a statement. Contradiction is a way to prove one.

    See also: negation, irrational number, rational number, lowest terms, prime number, proof

    proof by deduction Proof Year 1

    A way to prove a statement. Start from known facts or definitions, then use algebra and logic, step by step, to reach the result.

    Examples:Prove that the sum of two consecutive integers is odd.Call them n and n+1. Then n+(n+1)=2n+1.This is 2 times an integer plus 1, so it is odd.

    Watch out: Use a different letter for each number that can vary. If two even numbers are 2a and 2b, do not call both of them 2a.

    See also: proof, even number, odd number, consecutive integers, proof by exhaustion

    proof by exhaustion Proof Year 1

    A proof that splits every possibility into a small number of cases, then checks each case.

    Examples:Show that n2+n is even for every integer n.Case 1: n is even. Then n2 and n are both even, and even plus even is even.Case 2: n is odd. Then n2 and n are both odd, and odd plus odd is even.Every integer is even or odd, so the proof is complete.

    Watch out: The cases must cover every possibility, with no gaps. Trying a few values of n is not exhaustion.

    See also: proof, proof by deduction, even number, odd number

    proportional (∝) Algebra and functions Year 1

    Two quantities are linked so that the first is always the same fixed number times the second. The sign ∝ reads "is proportional to".

    Examples:y∝x means y=kx for a constant k. The graph is a straight line through the origin.y∝x2 means y=kx2. The graph of y against x2 is a straight line through the origin.

    Watch out: A straight line is proportional only if it goes through the origin. y=2x+3 is not proportional to x.

    Flip it: Inverse proportion is the opposite kind of link: when one grows, the other shrinks.

    See also: inversely proportional, reciprocal graph

    Pythagorean identity, sin² + cos² = 1 Trigonometry Year 1

    For any angle, the sine of the angle squared plus the cosine of the angle squared equals 1.

    Examples:sin2θ+cos2θ=1If sinθ=35 and θ is acute, then cos2θ=1−925=1625, so cosθ=45.

    Watch out: sin2θ means (sinθ)2. After taking a square root, there are two signs: use the CAST diagram to choose the right one.

    Flip it: It comes from Pythagoras on the Unit circle: the point (cosθ,sinθ) lies on x2+y2=1. Rearranged: cos2θ=1−sin2θ. For Year 2 versions, see Identity 1 + tan² = sec².

    See also: Trigonometric identity, Unit circle, Identity 1 + tan² = sec², Identity 1 + cot² = cosec²

    Q

    Q.E.D. Proof Year 1

    Letters written at the end of a proof, from the Latin for "which was to be shown". They tell the reader the proof is finished.

    Examples:2a+2b=2(a+b), which is even. Q.E.D.Some books use a small square □ instead of Q.E.D.

    Watch out: Write it only when you have reached exactly the result you were asked to prove. Q.E.D. does not fix a proof that has a gap.

    See also: proof, therefore (∴), show that

    quadratic Algebra and functions Year 1

    An expression or equation where the highest power of the unknown is 2, such as x squared plus 5x plus 4.

    Examples:x2+5x+4 is a quadratic expression.x2+5x+4=0 is a quadratic equation.The general form is ax2+bx+c with a≠0.

    Watch out: A quadratic must have an x2 term, so a cannot be 0. 5x+4 is not a quadratic.

    Flip it: Solving a quadratic gives its roots. Starting from the roots, you can build the quadratic.

    See also: discriminant, root (of an equation or function), completing the square, quadratic formula, parabola

    quadratic formula Algebra and functions Year 1

    A formula that gives the roots of a quadratic equation from its coefficients a, b and c.

    Examples:For ax2+bx+c=0: x=−b±b2−4ac2a.For 2x2+3x−1=0: x=−3±174.Read "±" as "plus or minus".

    Watch out: Write the equation as "something = 0" first. Write brackets round a negative b: for b=−3 the part b2 is (−3)2=9.

    Flip it: Completing the square on ax2+bx+c=0 proves the formula.

    See also: discriminant, completing the square, quadratic, root (of an equation or function)

    quadratic in disguise Algebra and functions Year 1

    An equation that is not a quadratic in x, but becomes one when you replace a power of x, or another expression, with a new letter.

    Examples:Solve x4−5x2+4=0. Let u=x2.Then u2−5u+4=0, so u=1 or u=4.So x2=1 or x2=4, which gives x=1, x=−1, x=2 or x=−2.

    Watch out: Finding u is only half of the work. Go back and solve for x. If u is negative and u=x2, there is no real x.

    See also: quadratic, root (of an equation or function)

    quartic Algebra and functions Year 1

    A polynomial of degree 4, or its graph. The highest power of x is 4.

    Examples:y=x4−5x2+4=(x−1)(x+1)(x−2)(x+2) has four roots.With a positive x4 coefficient, both ends of the graph go up.

    Watch out: A quartic can have 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4 real roots. Count a repeated root once when you count how many places the graph meets the axis.

    See also: polynomial, cubic, degree (of a polynomial)

    quotient Algebra and functions Year 1

    The result of a division, not counting any remainder.

    Examples:17=5×3+2: the quotient is 3 and the remainder is 2.x3+2x2−5x−6 divided by (x−2) has quotient x2+4x+3.

    See also: remainder, polynomial division

    Quotient law of logarithms Exponentials and logs Year 1

    The rule that subtracting two logarithms with the same base gives the logarithm of the first number divided by the second.

    Examples:logax−logay=logaxylog240−log25=log28=3. In particular loga1y=−logay.

    Watch out: The order matters: logax−logay is the logarithm of xy, not of yx. And logaxlogay is not logax−logay.

    See also: Product law of logarithms, Power law of logarithms, Logarithm (log)

    quotient rule Differentiation Year 2

    The rule for differentiating one function divided by another. Take the bottom times the derivative of the top, minus the top times the derivative of the bottom. Then divide by the bottom squared.

    Examples:If y=uv, then dydx=v×dudx−u×dvdxv2.For y=xx+1, let u=x and v=x+1. Then dydx=(x+1)×1−x×1(x+1)2=1(x+1)2.

    Watch out: The order of the subtraction matters. Write the bottom times the derivative of the top first. You can also write the fraction as a product with a negative power and use the product rule.

    See also: product rule, chain rule

    R

    R-form (harmonic form) Trigonometry Year 2

    A way to write a sin x + b cos x as one wave, such as R sin(x + α). From it you can see the greatest value and where it happens.

    Examples:asinx+bcosx=Rsin(x+α), where R=a2+b2 and tanα=ba, for positive a and b and acute α.Write 3sinx+4cosx as Rsin(x+α). R=9+16=5. tanα=43, so α=53.1°. The expression equals 5sin(x+53.1°).Its greatest value is 5, when x+53.1°=90°, that is x=36.9°. Its least value is −5.

    Watch out: Expand Rsin(x+α) with the Addition formulae (compound angle formulae) to get Rcosα=a and Rsinα=b. Check the signs of a and b before choosing α. R is the Amplitude of the new wave. R is always positive.

    Flip it: The same expression can be written as Rcos(x−α), with the same R and a different α.

    See also: Addition formulae (compound angle formulae), Amplitude, Double-angle formulae

    Radian Trigonometry Year 2

    A unit for measuring angles. One unit is the angle at the centre of a circle that cuts off an arc as long as the radius.

    Examples:The whole circle is 2×π radians, so 180°=π radians and 1 radian is about 57.3°.To change degrees to radians, multiply by π180. So 60°=π3 radians. To change radians to degrees, multiply by 180π.In radians the periods are 2×π for sinx and cosx, and π for tanx.

    Watch out: Radians are the default in calculus. Three results only work in radians: the derivative of sin x, Arc length and the Small-angle approximation. Check your calculator mode. When an angle has no unit, such as sin2, it is in radians.

    Flip it: A degree is 1360 of a full turn. A radian is defined using the circle itself, which is why the formulae are simpler.

    See also: Arc length, Area of a sector, Small-angle approximation, Arc

    Radius Coordinate geometry Year 1

    The distance from the centre of a circle to any point on it. The plural is radii.

    Example: (x−2)2+(y−1)2=4 has r2=4, so the radius is r=2.

    Watch out: The number on the right of the equation is r2, not r. Take the square root. For x2+y2=9 the radius is 3, not 9. A radius is a length, so it is positive.

    Flip it: The radius is the distance from the centre to a point on the circle, so you can find it with the Distance between two points formula.

    See also: Circle, Diameter, Centre of a circle, Tangent and radius at right angles

    range (of a function) Algebra and functions Year 2

    The set of output values a function gives, as the input takes every value in its domain.

    Examples:f(x)=x2 with domain all real numbers has range f(x)≥0.f(x)=x2, x≥1 has range f(x)≥1.

    Watch out: In statistics, "range" means largest value minus smallest value. For a function it is the set of all outputs.

    Flip it: The range of f is the domain of the inverse function f−1.

    See also: domain, function, inverse function

    Range of validity Sequences and series Year 2

    The values of x for which an infinite expansion gives the true value of the function. For (1 + x) to a power that is not a positive whole number, the range is -1 < x < 1.

    Examples:(1+2x)−3 is valid when |2x|<1, so when |x|<12.|x|<12 means −12<x<12.

    Watch out: Write the whole of the term you are expanding inside the modulus. For (2+x)−1=12(1+x2)−1, the condition is |x2|<1, so |x|<2, not |x|<1.

    See also: Binomial expansion for any rational power

    rate of change Differentiation Year 1

    How fast one quantity changes compared with another. When y depends on x, it is the gradient of the graph of y on the vertical axis against x on the horizontal axis, written dy by dx.

    Examples:If s metres is the distance after t seconds, dsdt is the speed in metres per second.If the volume V of water in a tank changes with time t, dVdt is the rate at which the volume changes.

    Watch out: The units of the rate are the units of y per unit of x. A negative rate of change means the quantity is getting smaller. A rate at one moment is the gradient of the tangent there, not an average.

    Flip it: Integrating a rate of change gives the total change in the quantity.

    See also: derivative, connected rates of change, gradient of a curve

    rational number Proof Year 1

    A number that can be written as one integer divided by another integer that is not zero.

    Examples:0.75=34 and 5=51 are rational.So is the recurring decimal 0.333…, which equals 13.

    Watch out: Every recurring decimal is rational, and so is every integer.

    Flip it: A number that cannot be written this way is irrational number.

    See also: irrational number, integer, lowest terms

    rationalise the denominator Algebra and functions Year 1

    Rewrite a fraction so that its bottom contains no surd. Multiply the top and the bottom by the same expression, chosen to remove the surd.

    Examples:13=1×33×3=3312+3=2−3(2+3)(2−3)=2−34−3=2−3

    Watch out: Multiply the top and the bottom by the same thing. The fraction then keeps its value, because you multiplied by 1. For 2+3 use 2−3, not 2+3.

    See also: surd, conjugate (of a surd expression)

    real number (ℝ) Algebra and functions Year 1

    Any number that has a place on the number line. Rational and irrational numbers are both real. The set of all real numbers is written ℝ.

    Examples:3, −0.5, 2 and π are real numbers.Other letters: ℤ for the integers and ℚ for the rational numbers.x∈ℝ means "x is any real number".

    Watch out: The square root of a negative number is not a real number. So x is real only for x≥0.

    See also: element of (∈), set notation, domain, range (of a function)

    reciprocal graph Algebra and functions Year 1

    The graph of y equals a over x, or y equals a over x squared. It has two branches, and the two axes are its asymptotes.

    Examples:y=1x has one branch in the top right and one in the bottom left.y=1x2 has both branches above the x-axis.

    Watch out: The graph has no point at x=0. The reciprocal of 0 does not exist.

    See also: asymptote, inversely proportional

    Recurrence relation Sequences and series Year 2

    An equation that gives each term of a sequence from the one before it, together with the starting value.

    Examples:un+1=2un+1, u1=3.Then u2=2×3+1=7, u3=2×7+1=15, u4=31.

    Watch out: Without the starting value the relation does not give one sequence. Work through the terms in order; you cannot skip to u10 without finding the ones before it.

    Flip it: Some recurrence relations settle on a limit. Replace both un and un+1 with L to find it.

    See also: Term-to-term rule, Limit of a sequence, Sequence notation, u_n

    Reducing to a straight line (linearising) Exponentials and logs Year 1

    Taking logarithms of both sides of an equation so that it turns into the equation of a straight line.

    Examples:y=axn becomes logy=nlogx+loga. A graph with logy on the vertical axis and logx on the horizontal axis is a straight line. See Log-log graph.y=kbx becomes logy=(logb)x+logk. A graph with logy on the vertical axis and x on the horizontal axis is a straight line. See Semi-log graph.

    Watch out: Match your equation to Y=mX+c term by term: say which expression is Y, which is X, which is m and which is c. Then read the gradient and the intercept from the graph.

    Flip it: Linearising is used to test experimental data: if the points lie on a straight line, the model fits the data.

    See also: Log-log graph, Semi-log graph, Power law of logarithms

    reflection (of a graph) Algebra and functions Year 1

    Flipping a graph over a line, like a mirror. The graph of y equals minus f of x is the reflection in the x-axis. The graph of y equals f of minus x is the reflection in the y-axis.

    Examples:y=−f(x) is the reflection of y=f(x) in the x-axis.y=f(−x) is the reflection in the y-axis.For f(x)=(x−2)2+1, the vertex is (2,1). The vertex of f(−x) is (−2,1).

    Watch out: A minus sign outside the function flips the graph up and down. A minus sign inside flips it left and right.

    See also: translation (of a graph), stretch (of a graph), inverse function

    region (of an inequality) Algebra and functions Year 1

    On a graph, all the points that make an inequality true. Its edge is the line or curve where the two sides are equal.

    Examples:y>2x−1: the region is above the line y=2x−1. Draw the line dashed, because points on it are not included.For y≤x2, draw the parabola solid and take the region on and below it.

    Watch out: A dashed edge is not included. A solid edge is included. Some questions ask you to shade the region you want. Others ask you to shade the region you do not want. Read the question.

    See also: inequality, simultaneous equations

    remainder Algebra and functions Year 1

    What is left over when you divide as far as you can. For a polynomial divided by a linear expression such as (x minus a), it is a number.

    Examples:17=5×3+2: the remainder is 2.x3+2x2−5x−6=(x−1)(x2+3x−2)−8: the remainder is −8.

    Watch out: When the remainder is 0, the divisor is a factor.

    See also: quotient, remainder theorem, polynomial division

    remainder theorem Algebra and functions Year 1

    When a polynomial f(x) is divided by (x minus a), the remainder is f(a). You get it by substituting a, with no division.

    Examples:f(x)=x3+2x2−5x−6. Divide by (x−1): the remainder is f(1)=1+2−5−6=−8.Divide by (x+3): the remainder is f(−3)=−27+18+15−6=0.

    Watch out: For (x+3) use a=−3. Substitute the number that makes the bracket zero, not the number in the bracket.

    Flip it: The factor theorem is the special case where the remainder is 0.

    See also: factor theorem, remainder, polynomial division

    repeated root Algebra and functions Year 1

    A root that comes from a factor that appears more than once. It is also called a double root when the factor appears twice.

    Examples:x2−6x+9=(x−3)2. The root x=3 is repeated, and the discriminant is 0.For y=(x−1)2(x+2), the root at 1 is repeated and the root at −2 is not.

    Watch out: At a double root the curve touches the x-axis and turns. It does not cross.

    Flip it: At a double root the x-axis is a tangent to the curve.

    See also: discriminant, root (of an equation or function), factor theorem

    Resultant Vectors Year 1

    The single vector that has the same effect as two or more vectors acting together: their sum.

    Example: The resultant of (31) and (24) is (55).

    Watch out: Find the resultant by adding components, then find its magnitude if you need the size.

    See also: Vector addition, Magnitude

    root (of an equation or function) Algebra and functions Year 1

    A value of x that makes a function equal zero. On the graph, it is where the curve meets the x-axis.

    Examples:For f(x)=x2−4x+3=(x−1)(x−3), the roots are x=1 and x=3.These are the solutions of f(x)=0.

    Watch out: A root of an equation is not the same as a square root, although the square roots of 5 are the roots of x2=5. Roots are always found where the graph meets the x-axis.

    Flip it: If a is a root of f, then (x−a) is a factor of f. See factor theorem.

    See also: quadratic, factor theorem, repeated root, discriminant

    S

    Scalar Vectors Year 1

    A quantity with size only and no direction: an ordinary number.

    Example: The numbers 5, −2 and 0.5 are scalars. So is a speed of 20 metres per second.

    Watch out: Speed is a scalar. Velocity is a vector, because it has a direction too. A scalar multiplies a vector, as in 3a.

    Flip it: A Vector has size and direction.

    See also: Vector, Scalar multiple

    Scalar multiple Vectors Year 1

    A vector multiplied by a number. Each component is multiplied by the number. The magnitude is multiplied by the size of the number, and the direction is reversed if the number is negative.

    Examples:3(2−1) = (6−3).−2(2−1) = (−42). It is twice as long and points the opposite way.

    Watch out: Multiply every component, not only the first.

    Flip it: If two vectors are scalar multiples of each other, they are parallel.

    See also: Scalar, Parallel vectors, Unit vector

    Secant (sec) Trigonometry Year 2

    1 divided by the cosine of an angle. This is the reciprocal of cosine.

    Examples:secx=1cosx. For example sec(60°)=11/2=2.The graph has vertical asymptotes where cosx=0, at x=90°, 270° and so on. It never takes a value strictly between −1 and 1 (its values are 1 or more, or −1 or less).

    Watch out: Here secant means the trigonometric function, not a secant line of a circle. Do not confuse sec with cos−1 (the inverse cosine, Inverse cosine (arccos, cos−¹)). Reciprocal means 1 divided by the number, but the inverse means the reverse function.

    See also: Cosine (cos), Cosecant (cosec), Cotangent (cot), Identity 1 + tan² = sec²

    second derivative Differentiation Year 1

    The derivative of the derivative. It tells you how fast the gradient is changing.

    Examples:For y=x3: dydx=3x2.Differentiate again: d2ydx2=6x, read as "d two y by dx squared". In function notation it is f″(x).At x=2 the second derivative is 12. It is positive, so the gradient is increasing there.

    Watch out: d2ydx2 does not mean (dydx)2. It means differentiate twice. A positive second derivative means the gradient is increasing. A negative one means the gradient is decreasing.

    See also: derivative, nature of a stationary point, convex, concave, point of inflection

    Sector Trigonometry Year 2

    A slice of a circle, bounded by two radii and the arc between them.

    Example: A sector with angle θ at the centre of a circle of radius r has an arc of length rθ. Its perimeter is 2r+rθ.

    Watch out: The perimeter of a sector includes the two straight radii as well as the arc. Do not leave them out.

    See also: Area of a sector, Arc, Arc length, Segment of a circle

    Segment of a circle Trigonometry Year 2

    The region of a circle cut off by a straight line (a chord), between the chord and the arc.

    Examples:A sector has radius r and angle θ in radians. The triangle inside it, made by the two radii and the chord, has area 12r2sinθ.So the area of the segment is 12r2θ−12r2sinθ=12r2(θ−sinθ).

    Watch out: A segment is not a sector. A sector reaches the centre; a segment is cut off by the chord. Subtract the triangle from the sector to get the segment.

    See also: Sector, Arc, Area of a sector

    self-inverse function Algebra and functions Year 2

    A function that is its own inverse. Applying it twice returns the starting value.

    Examples:f(x)=5−x: ff(x)=5−(5−x)=x.f(x)=1x, for x≠0, is also self-inverse.

    Watch out: Check ff(x) equals x for every x in the domain. The graph is unchanged by reflection in the line y=x.

    See also: inverse function, composite function

    Semi-log graph Exponentials and logs Year 1

    A graph with log y on the vertical axis and x on the horizontal axis. It is a straight line when y = k b to the power x, with gradient log b and vertical intercept log k.

    Examples:y=2×3x gives logy=(log3)x+log2. The gradient is log3=0.477 and the intercept is log2=0.301.With natural logarithms: y=Aekx gives lny=kx+lnA. The gradient is k and the intercept is lnA.

    Watch out: The gradient is logb, not b. Only the y-values are changed to logarithms. The x-values stay as they are.

    Flip it: It turns exponential growth or decay into a straight line, while a Log-log graph does the same for a power law.

    See also: Reducing to a straight line (linearising), Log-log graph, Exponential model

    separable differential equation Integration Year 2

    A first-order differential equation that can be rearranged so that every y is on one side with dy, and every x is on the other side with dx.

    Examples:dydx=xy. Separate: 1ydy=xdx.Integrate both sides: ln(|y|)=x22+c. So y=Aex2/2.

    Watch out: Put a constant on one side only. Dividing by an expression in y hides any solution where that expression is zero. Here, y=0 also satisfies the equation, and it is covered by A=0.

    See also: differential equation, general solution, particular solution

    Sequence Sequences and series Year 2

    A list of numbers in a fixed order that follows a rule.

    Example: 3, 7, 11, 15 … (add 4 each time). 1, 2, 4, 8 … (double each time).

    Watch out: Order matters. 1, 2, 3 and 3, 2, 1 are different sequences. A sequence may stop (it is finite) or go on for ever (it is infinite).

    See also: Term of a sequence, nth term (position-to-term rule), Term-to-term rule, Series

    Sequence notation, u_n Sequences and series Year 2

    The letter u with a small n below it means the term in position n. The next term is u with n + 1 below it. Some books use a or x instead of u.

    Examples:In 3, 7, 11, 15 …: u1=3 and u3=11.un+1 is the term after un.

    Watch out: un+1 is the next term. It is not un+1, which is one more than the term un.

    See also: Term of a sequence, nth term (position-to-term rule), Recurrence relation

    Series Sequences and series Year 2

    The sum of the terms of a sequence.

    Example: The sequence 2, 4, 6, 8 gives the series 2+4+6+8=20.

    Watch out: A sequence is a list. A series is the sum of that list. In everyday speech "a series of events" means a list, not a sum.

    See also: Sequence, Sum of the first n terms, S_n, Sigma notation

    set notation Algebra and functions Year 1

    A way to write a collection of numbers using curly brackets. Either list the members, or describe them with a rule.

    Examples:{1, 2, 3} is the set containing 1, 2 and 3.{x: x>2} is read "the set of all x such that x is greater than 2".{x: x>2} also means the interval (2, ∞).

    Watch out: The colon (or a vertical line) reads "such that". Order and repeats do not matter in a set.

    See also: element of (∈), interval, interval notation, union (∪), real number (ℝ)

    show that Proof Year 1

    A command word: the result is given, and you must prove it by writing every step of the working.

    Examples:Show that (x+1)2−(x−1)2=4x.Left side: x2+2x+1−(x2−2x+1)=4x. The left side equals the right side, so the result is shown.

    Watch out: Do not start from the result and treat it as already true. Start from one side and reach the other, step by step.

    See also: hence, proof, Q.E.D.

    Sigma notation Sequences and series Year 2

    The Greek capital letter sigma means "add up". The numbers below and above it say where to start and where to stop. The expression after it says what to add.

    Examples:∑r=142r=2+4+6+8=20. Read it as "the sum of 2r for r from 1 to 4".∑r=36r2=9+16+25+36=86.

    Watch out: The number of terms is the top minus the bottom, plus 1. The letter r is only a counter. The expression can be a constant: ∑r=145=5+5+5+5=20, which is 5×4.

    See also: Series, Sum of the first n terms, S_n

    simultaneous equations Algebra and functions Year 1

    Two or more equations that must be true at the same time. The solution is the set of values that fits all of them.

    Examples:Solve y=2x+1 and y=x2−2.Then x2−2=2x+1, so x2−2x−3=0 and x=3 or x=−1.Substitute each x into y=2x+1: the solutions are (3,7) and (−1,−1).

    Watch out: Pair each x with its own y. Do not mix them: two x-values and two y-values make four pairings, but only two are solutions. Check each pair in both equations.

    Flip it: On a graph, the solutions are the points where the two graphs meet.

    See also: quadratic, discriminant

    Sine (sin) Trigonometry Year 1

    In a right-angled triangle, the opposite side divided by the hypotenuse. For any angle, the y-coordinate of the matching point on the unit circle.

    Examples:A right-angled triangle has a 30° angle and hypotenuse 10. The side opposite the angle is 10 × sin 30° = 5, because sin(30°)=12.On the Unit circle, the point at 150° has y-coordinate sin(150°)=12. The sine of an obtuse angle is still positive.

    Watch out: Sine needs an angle after it: write sinx, never sin on its own. Check your calculator is in degrees or in radians to match the question. sin2x means (sinx)2.

    Flip it: The reverse question is "which angle has this sine?". That is the Inverse sine (arcsin, sin−¹) function, and it gives only one answer (the Principal value).

    See also: Cosine (cos), Tangent (tan), the trigonometric function, Unit circle, Cosecant (cosec), Inverse sine (arcsin, sin−¹)

    Sine rule Trigonometry Year 1

    In any triangle, each side divided by the sine of its opposite angle gives the same number.

    Examples:In triangle ABC, the side a is opposite angle A, b is opposite B and c is opposite C. Then asinA=bsinB=csinCFind side a when A = 40°, B = 65° and b = 12. asin(40°)=12sin(65°), so a=12sin(40°)sin(65°)=8.51 to 3 significant figures.

    Watch out: Use it only when you know a side and the angle opposite it (a matching pair), plus one more side or angle. To find an angle, turn the rule upside down: sinAa=sinBb. With two sides and a non-matching angle, see the Ambiguous case.

    Flip it: When there is no matching pair, use the Cosine rule instead.

    See also: Cosine rule, Ambiguous case, Area of a triangle, ½ab sin C

    Small-angle approximation Trigonometry Year 2

    For an angle close to 0, measured in radians, sine and tangent are nearly equal to the angle. Cosine is nearly 1 minus half the angle squared.

    Examples:For small θ in radians: sinθ ≈ θ, tanθ ≈ θ and cosθ ≈ 1−θ22. The sign ≈ is read as "is approximately equal to".For θ=0.1: sin0.1=0.09983, which is close to 0.1. And cos0.1=0.99500, and 1−0.012=0.995.

    Watch out: The angle must be in radians. The smaller the angle, the better the approximation. For θ=1 it is poor: sin1=0.84.

    Flip it: This is the same fact as limθ→0sinθθ=1, read as "the limit of sin theta over theta, as theta tends to 0, is 1". The derivative of sin x uses this fact.

    See also: Radian, Sine (sin), Cosine (cos), Tangent (tan), the trigonometric function

    Staircase diagram Numerical methods Year 2

    A graph of y = g(x) and y = x that shows an iteration as steps like a staircase. The steps stay on one side of the fixed point and move towards it or away from it.

    Examples:To draw it: start at x0 on the x-axis. Go up (or down) to the curve y=g(x). Go across to the line y=x. Go up (or down) to the curve again. Repeat.The x-coordinates where you meet the line y=x are x1, x2, x3. They steadily approach the fixed point.

    Watch out: A staircase appears when the curve slopes upwards at the fixed point (positive gradient). If the curve slopes downwards, you get a Cobweb diagram instead. Steps that move away from the fixed point show divergence.

    See also: Cobweb diagram, Convergence, Divergence, Fixed point

    Starting value Numerical methods Year 2

    The first approximation, x with subscript 0, from which an iteration begins.

    Examples:For x3−x−1=0, there is a root between 1 and 2, so you might choose x0=1.5.A change of sign usually gives a good starting value.

    Watch out: A poor starting value can send an iteration to a different root or make it fail. With Newton-Raphson method, do not start where the gradient is 0.

    See also: Iteration, Change of sign, Newton-Raphson method

    statement Proof Year 1

    A sentence that is either true or false, never both.

    Examples:"The number 7 is prime" is a true statement."x2=4" is true for some values of x and false for others. It becomes a statement once you say which x you mean.

    Watch out: A question such as "What is 7 plus 2?" is not a statement, because it is neither true nor false.

    See also: proof, conjecture, negation

    stationary point Differentiation Year 1

    A point on a curve where the gradient is zero, so the tangent is horizontal.

    Example: For y=x3−3x: dydx=3x2−3=0, so x=1 or x=−1. The stationary points are (1, -2) and (-1, 2).
