    Watch out: Solving dydx=0 gives only the x-values. Put each one into the original equation to find y. A stationary point is not always a maximum or minimum.

    See also: turning point, nature of a stationary point, maximum point, minimum point, point of inflection

    stretch (of a graph) Algebra and functions Year 1

    Making a graph taller, wider, shorter or narrower by a scale factor. A stretch works in one direction only.

    Examples:y=2f(x) stretches the graph vertically by scale factor 2. Roots stay where they are.y=f(2x) stretches it horizontally by scale factor 12. The graph is squashed towards the y-axis.For f(x)=x2−4: the roots of f(2x) are x=1 and x=−1.

    Watch out: A horizontal stretch uses the reciprocal. f(2x) halves the width. A vertical stretch uses the number as it is: y=2f(x) doubles the height.

    See also: translation (of a graph), reflection (of a graph)

    Strip width Numerical methods Year 2

    The width h of each strip in the trapezium rule, found by dividing the length of the interval by the number of strips.

    Examples:h=b−anHere a and b are the ends of the interval and n is the number of strips.From x=1 to x=3 with 4 strips: h=3−14=0.5. The x-values are 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3.

    Watch out: It is the number of strips that goes in the bottom of the fraction, not the number of y-values. 4 strips need 5 y-values.

    See also: Trapezium rule, Ordinate (y-value)

    Sum of the first n terms, S_n Sequences and series Year 2

    The total of the first n terms of a series, written with a capital S and a small n below it.

    Examples:For 2, 4, 6, 8 …: S3=2+4+6=12.For n of at least 2, each term is the difference of two sums: un=Sn−Sn−1. Here u3=S3−S2=12−6=6.

    Watch out: Sn is a total. un is one term. They are different numbers.

    See also: Series, Arithmetic series, Geometric series

    Sum to infinity Sequences and series Year 2

    The number that the sum of a geometric series settles on when you keep adding terms for ever. It exists only when r is between -1 and 1.

    Examples:S∞=a1−r for |r|<1.1+12+14 … has a=1, r=12, so S∞=11/2=2.8−4+2−1 … has r=−12, so S∞=83/2=163.

    Watch out: Check that |r|<1 first. If it is not, the series is divergent and has no sum to infinity. The word infinity does not mean the answer is infinite: it means you add infinitely many terms.

    Flip it: Why it works: as n grows, rn shrinks to 0 when |r|<1, so Sn gets closer to a1−r.

    See also: Geometric series, Convergent, Common ratio

    surd Algebra and functions Year 1

    A root that is an irrational number, such as the square root of 2. You leave it as a root to keep the answer exact.

    Examples:12=4×3=232×8=16=4. This answer is an integer, so it is no longer a surd.

    Watch out: 9=3, so it is not a surd. A calculator decimal such as 1.414 is only an approximation. "Give an exact answer" means keep the surd.

    Flip it: To remove a surd from the bottom of a fraction, rationalise the denominator.

    See also: rationalise the denominator, conjugate (of a surd expression), fractional index

    T

    Tangent Coordinate geometry Year 1

    A straight line that touches a circle at exactly one point and does not cross into the circle. For a curve, the tangent at a point is the straight line through that point with the same gradient as the curve there.

    Examples:Find the tangent to x2+y2=25 at (3, 4).The radius to (3, 4) has gradient 43. The tangent is perpendicular to it, so its gradient is −34.y−4=−34(x−3) gives 3x+4y=25.

    Watch out: A tangent to a circle meets it once. A tangent to another curve can cross the curve somewhere else, because it only has to match the curve at the point where it touches.

    Flip it: The Normal is the line at a right angle to the tangent at the same point.

    See also: Normal, Point of contact, Tangent and radius at right angles, Line meeting a circle

    Tangent (tan), the trigonometric function Trigonometry Year 1

    In a right-angled triangle, the opposite side divided by the adjacent side. It equals sine divided by cosine.

    Examples:In a right-angled triangle, a 45° angle has equal opposite and adjacent sides, so tan(45°)=1.On the Unit circle, tanθ is the gradient of the radius that makes angle θ with the positive x-axis.

    Watch out: The tangent function is not the tangent line to a curve or circle. The same word names two different ideas. tan(90°) does not exist, because the adjacent side is 0 and you cannot divide by 0. The graph of tan has vertical asymptotes there.

    Flip it: The reverse question is "which angle has this tangent?". That is Inverse tangent (arctan, tan−¹). The reciprocal 1tanx is called Cotangent (cot).

    See also: Sine (sin), Cosine (cos), The identity tan θ = sin θ / cos θ, Cotangent (cot), Inverse tangent (arctan, tan−¹)

    Tangent and radius at right angles Coordinate geometry Year 1

    A tangent to a circle is at a right angle to the radius drawn to the point of contact.

    Examples:The circle has centre (1, 2). The radius to the point (4, 6) has gradient 43.The tangent at (4, 6) has gradient −34.

    Watch out: The tangent is at a right angle to the radius to the point of contact, not to any radius.

    Flip it: The normal to a circle at a point lies along the radius to that point, so it passes through the centre.

    See also: Tangent, Radius, Normal, Point of contact

    tangent to a curve Differentiation Year 1

    The straight line that touches a curve at a point and has the same gradient as the curve there.

    Example: Find the tangent to y=x2 at (3, 9). The gradient is dydx=2x=6 at x=3. Use y−9=6(x−3). This gives y=6x−9.

    Watch out: Put the x-value into the derivative to get the gradient. Then use the original point in y−y1=m(x−x1). A tangent may cross the curve somewhere else.

    Flip it: The normal is the line at right angles to the tangent. See normal to a curve.

    See also: gradient of a curve, normal to a curve, derivative

    Term of a sequence Sequences and series Year 2

    One number in a sequence. The first term is the number in position 1, the second term is in position 2, and so on.

    Example: In 3, 7, 11, 15 … the first term is 3 and the third term is 11.

    Watch out: Count the first term as position 1, not 0, unless the question says otherwise.

    See also: Sequence, Sequence notation, u_n

    Term-to-term rule Sequences and series Year 2

    A rule that gives each term from the term before it.

    Example: Start at 3 and use "double and add 1": 3, 7, 15, 31 …

    Watch out: You need a starting term as well as the rule. The same rule with a different start gives a different sequence.

    Flip it: Written with symbols, a term-to-term rule is a Recurrence relation.

    See also: Recurrence relation, nth term (position-to-term rule)

    The identity tan θ = sin θ / cos θ Trigonometry Year 1

    The tangent of an angle equals its sine divided by its cosine, for every angle where cosine is not zero.

    Examples:tanθ=sinθcosθShow that sinθtanθ=cosθ. Replace tan: sinθ×cosθsinθ=cosθ.

    Watch out: It is not defined when cosθ=0, which is at 90°, 270° and so on. Use it to turn an equation with both sin and cos into one with only tan. To turn it into one with only sin or only cos, use the Pythagorean identity, sin² + cos² = 1.

    See also: Tangent (tan), the trigonometric function, Pythagorean identity, sin² + cos² = 1, Trigonometric identity

    The number e Exponentials and logs Year 1

    An irrational number, about 2.71828. It is the only base a for which the graph of y = a to the power x has gradient equal to its height at every point.

    Examples:e = 2.71828 to 5 decimal places. The digits never end and never repeat.At x=0, y=e0=1, and the gradient of y=ex there is also 1. At x=1, the height is e and the gradient is also e.

    Watch out: It is a number, like π, not a variable. Do not round it to 2.7 in an exact answer: leave it as e.

    Flip it: The Natural logarithm (ln) uses e as its base: lne=1.

    See also: Natural exponential function (e^x), Natural logarithm (ln)

    therefore (∴) Proof Year 1

    A sign that means "so" or "for this reason". It joins a reason to the result that follows from it.

    Examples:2x=8. ∴ x=4.

    Watch out: It is not an equals sign. It also does not mean "because": the reason comes before the sign, and the result comes after it.

    See also: implies (⇒), Q.E.D., proof

    Three-dimensional axes Vectors Year 2

    Three axes, x, y and z, all at right angles to each other and meeting at the origin. A point is given by three coordinates (x, y, z).

    Example: The point (2, 3, 4) is 2 along the x-axis, 3 along the y-axis and 4 up the z-axis. Its position vector is 2i+3j+4k.

    Watch out: The usual layout is right-handed. Turn from the x-axis to the y-axis the way a screw turns. The z-axis points the way the screw moves. Drawings of 3D axes show distances at an angle, so they are not to scale.

    See also: i, j and k notation, Distance in three dimensions, Position vector

    translation (of a graph) Algebra and functions Year 1

    Sliding the whole graph sideways or up and down, without turning or resizing it.

    Examples:y=f(x)+2 moves the graph of y=f(x) up by 2.y=f(x−3) moves it right by 3.The parabola y=x2 becomes y=(x−3)2+2, with its vertex at (3,2).

    Watch out: A number added inside the bracket moves the graph the opposite way. f(x+3) moves the graph left by 3.

    Flip it: A translation is undone by sliding the graph back by the same amount.

    See also: stretch (of a graph), reflection (of a graph), asymptote, vertex (of a parabola)

    Trapezium rule Numerical methods Year 2

    A method that estimates the area under a curve by dividing that area into strips of equal width and treating each strip as a trapezium.

    Examples:∫abydx ≈ h2[y0+yn+2∑r=1n−1yr]Here h is the strip width, n is the number of strips and y0 to yn are the y-values. The sign ≈ is read as "is approximately equal to". The sigma sign means "add up": here it adds y1 to yn−1.Estimate ∫02x2dx with 4 strips. h=2−04=0.5. The y-values are 0, 0.25, 1, 2.25 and 4. So the estimate is 0.52[0+2(0.25+1+2.25)+4]=0.25×11=2.75.

    Watch out: The first and last y-values are used once. All the middle ones are used twice. With n strips there are n+1 y-values. The answer is an estimate: say whether it is an over- or underestimate.

    Flip it: The exact answer is ∫02x2dx=83=2.667. So the estimate 2.75 is too big: see Over- and underestimate.

    See also: Strip width, Ordinate (y-value), Over- and underestimate, Numerical integration

    Trigonometric equation Trigonometry Year 1

    An equation where the unknown is an angle inside sin, cos or tan. You usually solve it for angles in a stated interval.

    Examples:Solve sin(2x)=0.5 for 0°≤x≤360°. First 2x lies in 0°≤2x≤720°, so 2x=30°,150°,390°,510°.So x=15°,75°,195°,255°.

    Watch out: Do not divide both sides by sinx or cosx: that function could be 0, so you lose those solutions. Move everything to one side and factorise instead. When the angle is 2x, work out the longer interval for 2x first, then halve.

    Flip it: A Trigonometric identity is true for every angle, so it is not solved: it is proved.

    See also: Principal value, CAST diagram, Trigonometric identity

    Trigonometric identity Trigonometry Year 1

    A statement about sine, cosine or tangent that is true for every angle where both sides have a value.

    Examples:sin2θ+cos2θ=1 is true for every angle θ. It is an identity. It is sometimes written with the sign ≡.sinθ=cosθ is true only for some angles, such as 45° and 225°. It is an equation, not an identity.

    Watch out: To prove an identity, start from one side and work towards the other, changing only that side. Do not move terms across the equals sign and do not treat the identity as an equation to solve. Where one side is undefined (such as tanθ at 90°), the identity does not apply.

    Flip it: To solve a Trigonometric equation, you find the few angles that make it true. To prove an identity, you show it is true for all of them.

    See also: Pythagorean identity, sin² + cos² = 1, The identity tan θ = sin θ / cos θ, Trigonometric equation

    turning point Differentiation Year 1

    A point where a curve changes from rising to falling, or from falling to rising. It is a maximum or a minimum.

    Example: The curve y=x2−4x turns at (2, -4). It falls before and rises after.

    Watch out: Every turning point of a smooth curve is a stationary point. The reverse is not true: on y=x3 the point (0, 0) is stationary, but the curve keeps rising, so it does not turn.

    See also: stationary point, maximum point, minimum point

    U

    union (∪) Algebra and functions Year 1

    The sign ∪ joins two sets into one set. The new set holds everything that is in either of them.

    Examples:Read A ∪ B as "A union B".x2>4 gives x<−2 or x>2.In interval notation: (-∞, -2) ∪ (2, ∞).

    Watch out: "And" gives only the numbers in both intervals (the intersection, ∩). "Or" gives the union.

    Flip it: The intersection ∩ is the reverse idea: only what is in both sets. For example, x>1 and x<5 give (1, 5).

    See also: interval notation, inequality, set notation

    Unit circle Trigonometry Year 1

    A circle with radius 1 and centre at the origin, used to define sine, cosine and tangent for angles of any size.

    Examples:Measure an angle θ anticlockwise from the positive x-axis. The point where the line at that angle meets the circle is (cosθ,sinθ).At θ=90° the point is (0, 1), so cos(90°)=0 and sin(90°)=1.

    Watch out: Angles measured clockwise are negative. Every point on the circle has x2+y2=1. This gives the Pythagorean identity, sin² + cos² = 1.

    See also: Sine (sin), Cosine (cos), Tangent (tan), the trigonometric function, Pythagorean identity, sin² + cos² = 1, CAST diagram

    Unit vector Vectors Year 1

    A vector with magnitude 1. To find the unit vector in the direction of a, divide a by its magnitude. It is written as a with a small hat over it, and read "a hat".

    Examples:For a=3i+4j: |a|=5, so a^=3i+4j5=0.6i+0.8j.Check: 0.62+0.82=1.

    Watch out: i and j are unit vectors, but they are not the only ones. Any direction has a unit vector.

    Flip it: Every vector is its magnitude times the unit vector in its direction: a=|a|a^.

    See also: Magnitude, i and j notation, Scalar multiple

    V

    Vector Vectors Year 1

    A quantity that has both a size and a direction. It is drawn as an arrow: the length shows the size and the arrow points the way.

    Example: A move of 3 across and 2 up is a vector. So is a displacement of 5 km due north.

    Watch out: Two vectors are equal when they have the same size and the same direction. Where the arrow is drawn does not matter.

    Flip it: A Scalar has size only.

    See also: Scalar, Column vector, Vector notation, Magnitude

    Vector addition Vectors Year 1

    Adding vectors by adding their components. In a drawing, start the second arrow at the head (the pointed end) of the first. The sum goes from the tail (the start) of the first arrow to the head of the second.

    Examples:(31) + (24) = (55).In a triangle ABC, AB→+BC→=AC→.

    Watch out: Adding vectors does not add the lengths unless the vectors point the same way. The order does not matter: a+b=b+a.

    Flip it: Subtracting undoes adding.

    See also: Resultant, Vector subtraction, Negative of a vector

    Vector notation Vectors Year 1

    Ways of writing a vector: a bold letter in print, a letter underlined by hand, or two letters with an arrow over them to show the start and end.

    Examples:In print, a bold a. By hand, a underlined.AB→ is the vector that goes from A to B.

    Watch out: The order of the letters matters. AB→ goes from A to B. BA→ goes the other way, so BA→=−AB→.

    See also: Vector, Negative of a vector, Position vector

    Vector proof Vectors Year 1

    A proof in geometry that uses vectors. Write the sides of a shape as vectors and combine them. Then show that two vectors are parallel, collinear or in a given ratio.

    Examples:In triangle OAB, M is the midpoint of OA and N is the midpoint of OB. Let OA→=a and OB→=b.MN→=MO→+ON→=−12a+12b=12(b−a)=12AB→.So MN is parallel to AB and half its length.

    Watch out: Choose two vectors from one corner as a and b, and write every other vector using them. Finish with a sentence that says what you have shown.

    See also: Collinear, Parallel vectors, Point dividing a line in a ratio, Position vector

    Vector subtraction Vectors Year 1

    Finding the difference of two vectors by taking away their components one by one. It is the same as adding the negative of the vector you take away.

    Examples:(52) − (14) = (4−2).With position vectors, AB→=b−a. This is the end minus the start.

    Watch out: The order matters. b−a is the vector from A to B. a−b is the vector from B to A. Subtract every component, not only the first.

    See also: Vector addition, Negative of a vector, Position vector

    vertex (of a parabola) Algebra and functions Year 1

    The turning point of a parabola: its lowest point if it opens upwards, and its highest point if it opens downwards.

    Examples:y=(x−2)2−1 has its vertex at (2,−1).In general, y=a(x−p)2+q has its vertex at (p,q).

    Watch out: The bracket (x−2) gives x=2. The sign flips: take the number that makes the bracket zero.

    See also: completing the square, parabola, axis of symmetry

    W

    with respect to Integration Year 1

    The words that say which letter is the variable when you differentiate or integrate. In an integral, the letter after d is the variable.

    Example: In ∫3tdt, the variable is t and the answer is 32t2+c. In ∫3tdx, the variable is x, so t is a constant and the answer is 3tx+c.

    Watch out: The dx is not decoration. Every integral needs a dx, and its letter must match the variable in the integrand.

    See also: integrand, integrate

    Taught in: Integration as reverse differentiation

    X

    x-intercept Coordinate geometry Year 1

    The point where a line or curve meets the x-axis (it may cross it or only touch it). Its y-coordinate is always 0.

    Example: The line y=x−3: substitute y=0 to get 0=x−3, so x=3. The x-intercept is the point (3, 0).

    Watch out: A horizontal line such as y=2 never crosses the x-axis, so it has no x-intercept. A curve can have several.

    Flip it: The y-intercept is the same idea on the other axis: substitute x=0.

    See also: y-intercept

    Y

    y-intercept Coordinate geometry Year 1

    The point where a line or curve meets the y-axis (it may cross it or only touch it). Its x-coordinate is always 0.

    Example: The line y=12x+2: substitute x=0 to get y=2. The y-intercept is the point (0, 2).

    Watch out: In y=mx+c, the number c is the y-coordinate of the y-intercept. The intercept itself is the point (0, c).

    Flip it: The x-intercept is the same idea on the other axis: substitute y=0.

    See also: x-intercept, Equation of a straight line, y = mx + c

    Z

    Zero vector Vectors Year 1

    The vector with no length, written as a bold 0. All its components are 0.

    Example: AB→+BA→ is the zero vector: you end up back where you started.

    Watch out: It is a vector. It is not the same thing as the number 0. It has no direction.

    See also: Negative of a vector
